en: And this [object] is one whose true nature (*tattvārtha*) has not been examined, because it is superimposed by a conceptualizing cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*). The analysis of the compound is: that by which the object as a real entity (*vastvartha*) is disregarded as being the true nature.

Just as in the world, even that which has ascended to the intellect is perceived through the determination (*adhyavasita*) of its being that [very object], so too is that distinction between dharma and so forth; "in that way" means according to worldly perception. The connection [of the sentence] is: "the arrangement of the probandum and the probans is conceived by the learned."
For what purpose [is it] for others...?

[2] Furthermore, for what reason is the conventional usage of "oneness" and so forth impossible with respect to a real entity? To this he says: "They do not combine," and so forth. Ultimate objects do not combine *per se*; therefore, there is no conventional usage of a universal (*sāmānya*) with respect to a real entity. Nor are they differentiated by properties such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), because it is impossible for that single entity to possess multiplicity individually. And thus, among those many objects, form is one.
When multiple forms are determined with respect to a single object, that is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of the intellect.
...they do not differ; for that reason, the ultimate objects [are not distinct].
This is a commonality among many.
Likewise, regarding the distinction between phenomena (*dharma*) and their substrata (*dharmin*), this distinction—which is the conventional usage of diversity—is also [not ultimately real].

If it is asked, "Since the appearance in cognition is unreal, how can there be a distinction of properties such as being produced (*kṛtakatva*) with respect to that [appearance], given that the Buddhist object is not an external particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)," he says:
"And of that very [appearance]," and so forth.
This means that this is said with respect to the appearance in cognition itself, because of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of its identity with the external object.
4 /// ...just as even for one who has come to see that [object], the appearance of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa-pratibhāsa*) is determined;
for this very reason it is said, "it is conceptualized" (*prakalpyate*).

Why is it that, just as the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the thing itself is grasped by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the specific characteristic itself—qualified by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) such as impermanence, which is inferred through a means of proof (*sādhana*)—is not likewise grasped?
Thus he says "the probandum," and so forth.
Since there is a loss of the perception of reality in this conceptual construction that "this is the probandum" and "this is the proof," how could [one's own... arise?

5 /// ... because of the statement that "the particular (bheda) qualified by the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) is apprehended," [some might] suspect that the Teacher Diṅnāga and others have asserted the apprehension of the particular-characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) as conjoined with the universal (sāmānya). Dispelling this suspicion, he says "the particular" and so forth.

The meaning is: even in this statement that "the particular conjoined with the universal is cognized," the particular-characteristic itself is not what is to be grasped; it is not to be understood in such a way that the particular-characteristic alone is being indicated.
... indeed for those who have accumulated supernatural powers (ṛddhi)... [bhavet] ///
One should understand that even in that case, they are grasped as "perceived.
Others, however, read it with the masculine gender: "particularity (bheda) and generality (sāmānya), conjoined, are the object of apprehension. In that context, the meaning is "particularity."
Even in this statement that "the object of apprehension is that which is mixed with the universal," the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not to be understood [as the object].
If one asks what the reason is for it being understood in that way, he says "common" (*samāna*), etc.
Because there is oneness in the manifold...

In that [conceptual construction], there is a multiplicity of attributes (*upādhi*) and a variety of forms; by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the forms of the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) is intended.

That [object] cannot in any way be grasped as a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Why? Because in that single particular characteristic—which has the nature of being produced, impermanence, and so forth—there is no connection with the many distinct properties (*dharma*), namely, the various distinctions consisting of the essential forms of things, within that single particular characteristic.
For it is not logical that there should be many real forms within a single entity, because a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is partless (*niraṃśatvāt*).
"...there is no word that expresses its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) by way of its uncommon form, nor is there any conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). This is the context.
The meaning is that even conceptual construction, which grasps the specific characteristic by way of its uncommon form, does not exist.

Why? Because words and conceptual constructions function only through universals (*sāmānya*); therefore, for one who says that there is no word expressing that [specific characteristic], [it follows that] regarding the specific characteristic...
“Furthermore,” and so forth.
Since it was stated immediately prior that [the word] does not function by means of a universal (*sāmānya*) alone, this objection is improper.

This is true; however, this presentation is intended to state an additional refutation. That which is made an object by convention (*saṃketa*) is the conventionalized (*saṃketita*); words denote that for the sake of practical usage (*vyavahāra*). That is what is traditionally known as “convention” (*saṃketa*).

That specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) in which it is intended that a convention (*saṃketa*) is made does not exist at the time of linguistic usage (*vyavahārakāla*), for [the convention] was not made [at that time].
...because [the universal] cannot occur in another individual (*vyaktyantara*). Even that single individual which is intended as the object of convention (*saṃketaviṣaya*) is momentary;
therefore, there is no persistence (*anugama*) of that same form at a later time, much less in another individual distinct in space and time.

For this reason, the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) "convention is not made with respect to that particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)" is to be supplied. He explains this with the words beginning "for not" (*na hi*).
"Previously" means at the time of making the convention.
B. *Pramāṇavārttikaṭīkā* r1 /// ... some entity ... elsewhere, i.e., where it would have to manifest in a different individual;
and this [property of] "being elsewhere" is not possible for a universal that is an actual entity—this is the connection.

What is the reason? Because if it were admitted that [the transformation] is not other than its substratum, there would be no continuity; for that which is non-distinct from one thing and constitutes its very essence... [cannot undergo change].
Because the state of being a substratum has been refuted;

if, due to the lack of connection with a universal that is distinct [from individuals], it does not produce a cognition of its own form in another individual, then this is equally true for the first individual as well— so why say "in previously unperceived individuals"?
It should simply be stated as "in individuals.
Likewise, one should not say, "because what is seen in one place cannot possibly be seen elsewhere," for even in a single location, there is a distinction between individuals...
3 /// ... the perception of a universal elsewhere is not possible... because no other mode [of existence] is possible apart from identity (*tattva*) and difference (*anyatva*).
Thus he says, "For the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)," and so forth. The connection is that [the universal] does not transcend either identity with or difference from the intrinsic nature.
Why? Because a form (*rūpa*) that is not that [nature], being of a different character, does not escape its difference [from it].
The meaning is "because it is other than that.
Let it be that it does not have that nature; but why is it other? ... [text missing] ... why is it other?
The meaning is that [it] has the characteristic of being other,
like another aspect;
the suffix -vati is used here in the sense of the genitive case.

For instance, since even suffering is distinct from pleasure by virtue of its being non-pleasurable—that is, simply because suffering is not of the nature of pleasure—the pervasion has been stated by this much, namely, by the characteristic of being distinct from that [nature].
And since this characteristic of being distinct is without distinction, the property (dharma) has been stated by this very [reason] even with respect to the intended generality.
The formal argument (*prayoga*), however, is as follows: whatever, while being a real entity, is not of that nature, is distinct from it, just as [suffering is distinct] from pleasure.

5 /// ... because the conventional usage of "otherness" is what is to be proven, [the reason] is indeed a *svabhāvahetu*. Thus, first of all, if the universal (*sāmānya*) does not possess that form [of the individual], otherness follows as a consequence. Now, if otherness is not accepted, then it follows that [the universal] is identical [to the individual]; thus he says "And that," etc. If it were non-different from the manifestation (*vyakti*), then that very universal would be of the same form as the manifestation itself.

If it were non-real (*atatva*), then because its nature would be that of non-manifestation, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of its being something else, like any other entity; and this has been stated immediately prior. Let it be non-different; [as for] the universal... [the rest of the sentence is fragmentary].

6 /// ... [the term] "pervasion" (anugama) means the entry of one individual essence into another individual, that is to say, the state of having the nature of another individual. Why? Because it would follow that what is not pervaded would not be another individual.
If the universal consisting of a *śābaleya* cow were to become the very self-nature of a *bāhuleya* cow, then the *bāhuleya* would have arisen as nothing other than a *śābaleya*.
Since it is not distinct from the universal that consists of the *śābaleya* [cow], how could it—like the *śābaleya* itself—be considered a different individual from that? ... ///
[The cognition] does not follow from a universal that is distinct [from the individual], nor does it follow from one that is non-distinct.

The subject under discussion is that "the cognition follows from a universal. Why? Because that distinct universal has no basis—that is, it does not subsist—in any particular individual; for subsistence is impossible without a relation. Subsistence means being contained (*ādheyatā*), and since an individual is the locus of manifestation, it is not tenable [for the universal] to subsist in it, and so forth. Furthermore, [this refutes] the relationship between the manifested and the manifestor, as well as the relationship of container and contained.
If it is argued that "the relationship between the universal (*sāmānya*) and its possessor (*tadvat*) will exist," [the author] says: "Of another as well," and so forth.

In the phrase "of the state of the manifested and the manifestor (*vyaṅgyavyañjakabhāva*), etc.," the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is used; by the word "etc.," the relationship of container and contained (*ādhārādheyabhāva*) is included.
From this—referring to the two types of relationships previously refuted—[it follows that] there would also be another [relationship] for whatever...
Because no universal exists with respect to the manifestation (*vyakti*) of any particular relation, for what reason? Because it is eternal;

since a universal cannot be assisted by any particular manifestation, there is no connection [between them], for it has been stated that there is no connection whatsoever for that which lacks a causal dependence (*apratibandha*).
By this, the portion of the verse beginning with "because of the lack of dependence when there is difference" has been explained.

If it is argued that even though it lacks a connection, the universal produces a cognition that conforms to the universal among the individuals, [the author] says "because of the lack of connection," and so forth.
The meaning is "thus.
"That" means "therefore.
"This" refers to the proponent of the general [view].

Because of the observation of a single universal as the cause, one who does not desire the occurrence elsewhere—in another individual—of that cognition which occurs in a single individual such as a brindled cow, cannot transcend the identity or difference [of that universal] from the individual, since there is no other possible mode of being for a real entity (*vastu*), and the fault in that case has already been stated; thus, this is untenable.
[The cognition] follows from a universal that is a real entity...

The cognition [of a single form] in respect to diverse things is indeed an error, because it functions by superimposing non-difference upon what is different. From where, then, does it arise? To this he says, "by conceptual construction," and so forth.

That latent impression (*vāsanā*), which by its very nature produces such a conceptual construction through the experience of objects excluded from those of a different class, has been deposited; it arises from that. And since this has already been stated previously, he says, "the difference between entities," and so forth, referring to entities—that is, their effects.
The difference from those things that do not produce that effect, and likewise for those things that are so constituted...

This has already been thoroughly examined above. In that context, two things were presented: the distinction between entities (*bhāvabheda*) as the indirect cause, and the nature of latent impressions (*vāsanāprakṛti*) as the direct cause.
[The opponent asks: "If the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) alone is what is expressed by words, then how is it that... and so forth.

The terms "effect" (kārya) applied to the *pradhāna*, the Lord (*īśvara*), and so forth—such as "the world is the effect of the *pradhāna*" or "the world is the effect of the Lord"—include, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), terms such as "the transformation of the *śabdabrahman*.
[This applies] to internal and external entities (*bhāva*) which, being not that [in reality], are unproduced...
5 /// ... then there would be a distinction consisting of the effects of *pradhāna* and so forth;
that very thing is the non-distinction of all. By means of that cause of non-distinction, they function everywhere.

And that [universal] does not exist among entities according to the view of the proponent of *anyāpoha*, because [entities] consist of effects such as non-primordial matter (*apradhāna*) and so forth.
Therefore, how could they function without distinction toward things of such a nature?
The intended meaning is: "Not at all."
And thus, the point is that the determination of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) would be non-pervasive.
He refutes this with the words "those too" (*te 'pi*), etc.
Those...

6 /// ... and so forth. Because the continuum of consciousness has been refined through transformation (*pariṇāma*) regarding the entity as it is not [as it appears], in the perceptions and experiences of all external and internal objects...
Even when [the causes] exist, disregarding their distinction, [it arises] from the non-primary cause...

...the meaning is "it will be seen. Likewise, through determination (*adhyavasāya*), even though things are not the primary effects, because one determines them as being the primary effects of *pradhāna*,
consciousness— which is not actually so [but] imagined as the primary effect of *pradhāna*— is likewise imagined.
By the exclusion of that [other], there is an absence of the primary object; thus,
that very object which appears to the conceptualizing consciousness is itself "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) by way of excluding conceptualizations of a different class.
...the source, the origin, the arising of which conceptual construction; from that [construction] it has arisen. This is what is meant:

even if there is indeed no such differentiation in reality, nevertheless, exclusion (anyāpoha) as superimposed by conceptual construction is the very factor for the operation of words; therefore, there is no fault of lack of pervasion.
[The effect of] Primordial Matter (pradhāna) and so forth...
The intention is that since the universal is refuted in both ways— both in the case of the elements and in the case of effects that are not primary—
the proponent of the theory of the exclusion of others (anyāpohavādin), however, incurs no such fault; thus he says:

The meaning of "tathā" and so forth is: by way of conceptualizing [them] as the effects of the primary [cause], the Pradhāna; [this is said] in contrast to those other things conceptualized as the effects of non-primary [causes].
It refers to the distinction regarding those things upon which the status of being the effect of the Pradhāna and so forth has been superimposed.

[The opponent asks: "Is it not the case that the universal is the cause for the application [of a term] based on conditions? [The author replies: This is not so; because even by that proponent of the universal who postulates a universal, there must necessarily be admitted—in that very entity which is intended as the primary effect—a distinction from what is intended as a non-primary effect, since such a distinction is inseparable [from the universal].
For if the effect of the primary [cause] were not [different] from the person, which is the effect of the non-primary [cause]...
It is sufficient and capable [to establish] a single term's application and so forth with respect to the effect;

showing without distinction that just as the cognition of a universal is erroneous regarding differences that do not possess such [a common nature], so it is also regarding differences that do possess such [a common nature],
he says "If," and so forth.
The word "yadi" (if) is for the purpose of illuminating its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If its intrinsic nature is to be devoid of an object in all cases, then what [state] are we in?

Because that which is apprehended— such as impermanence and so forth, as well as permanence and so forth— is absent from external objects, and because this constitutes an apprehension of what is unreal, it is nothing but a distortion and nothing but an error; therefore, one need not pay any heed to defining the object of this universal cognition, since it is devoid of an [external] object.
If all cognition of universals is erroneous, how then is there correspondence with reality through inference? To this he says:

5 /// ... which we shall explain in the section on "Determination" (*pariccheda*), as was previously stated. Where there is a connection with a real entity (*vastu*)—as in the case of inference based on what has been stated, such as "just as...

and so forth—it is not because of the inclusion or apprehension of an object of cognition that consists of a real entity in its actual state that the conceptualization of inference (*anumāna-vikalpa*) achieves correspondence with the real entity (*vastu-saṃvāda*).
"Like perception" is an example by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta). For what reason? Because it is not so.
And because [the capacity] arises from that [perception], there is efficacy; this is the meaning here.
If the cognition of a universal (*sāmānyabuddhi*) is without an object, how can it be said that its object is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*)? To this he says "no," and so forth.

The ellipsis to be supplied is: "because this cognition of a universal arises through the power of perceiving distinct entities—that is, by the force of the experience of particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as excluded from those of a different class."
The inclusion of the term "frequently" (bahula) [is for the purpose of...]

[This occurs] because of the adherence [to the false view] that those distinct objects are real entities, due to the superimposition of the appearance within one's own consciousness onto the status of being external things.
The meaning is that [the mind] functions by unifying the perceived object and the conceptualized object.
This is what is meant: because it arises through the power of seeing distinct objects, and once arisen, it functions by superimposing its own appearance onto those distinct objects.
To that extent, some explain that there are two [distinct] arisings;
others, however, maintain that this is a single realization of two.

Because of the force of perceiving distinct objects, there is a determination (*adhyavasāya*) of existence within those self-appearances; thus, because of the determination that "the very self-appearance is a distinct entity," it is said to have difference as its object.
...there is no conceptualization [of things] such as a rabbit’s horn. If one asks how that is so, he says: "In the same way, existence," and so forth.

Just as cognitions of production and so on arise by the force of experiencing the apprehension of the intrinsic nature of distinct entities, and proceed by superimposing distinct existences upon their own internal reflections—even in the case of cognitions such as "the effect of Pradhāna" or "eternal"—it is the same regarding existence...

The state of having difference as its object (*bhedaviṣayatva*) is said [to belong] to the function [of conceptualization]. Even in conceptualizations such as "the horn of a hare," there is the state of having difference as its object because of the superimposition of difference through the exclusion of other conceptualizations. It resides only in the location of the individual (*vyakti*) that belongs to its own substrate, and not in a location devoid of individuals, nor is it omnipresent; for it exists even in locations devoid of individuals. [Regarding the phrase] *apūrvagha*... [the text continues].
The intention is that there is no such occurrence.

There might be an occurrence if, from that prior substance, its universal (*sāmānya*) were to pass over to the substance subsequently arising; however, since that [passing] does not exist, he says "for not," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "because it resides in another substance": this refers to the entity called the universal, which resides in a substance located in a different place than the substance about to arise, and which does not move from its previous substratum; therefore, [the universal cannot belong] to both...
But how could one who asserts that there is a connection with a mirror located in a different place not be insane?
[For] it is a deluded cognition produced by the power of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
There arises an appearance in a mirror that follows a reflection;

as it has been said regarding objects with opposing transformations, such as the surface of a diamond or a mirror, there is no possibility for entities whose nature is that of mountains and so forth [to exist there].
Even those who...

In a location devoid of individuals, because its presence there is not admitted; and later, when an individual has arisen, a universal exists [there], because an individual devoid of the universal is not admitted.
Furthermore, the location was not produced together with the individual, nor did it come from some previous particular individual.
And this does not go...
Since it is accepted that [the object] is not common [to all], there is a contradiction; and because that contradiction is difficult for the wise to endure, it is a "burden" (bhāra).
Therefore he says:
"Who would [do] this," and so forth.
For how could a wise person tolerate what is improper?

But the insentient [entity], being incapable of investigating what is logical or illogical due to its lack of knowledge, might even tolerate [the objection] on account of its dullness, as it says elsewhere: "Because of its insentience.
Let it be granted, then, that the universal is active; nevertheless...
[he] would go as one who has no share, having abandoned the prior pledge (ādhāra) which is without a share;
he says that neither of these two exists.
And so forth:

[the author] clarifies the portion of the sūtra beginning with "previously the substratum" by means of the *Miśraka*, stating that it is in a location different from the place where [the effect] intends to arise.
And regarding "of those two," this refers to the two substances produced earlier and later; [the phrase] "different," and so forth, [is used].
... [it is] connected with two substances through two locations.
For light, because it possesses parts, is connected with a jar by one part and with cloth and so forth by another;
likewise, ropes, bamboo, and staffs are also [connected] with their own respective relata.
The passage beginning with "na hi" and so forth is a justification for this very point.
To the question "Why is it not logical?", he says:
"tasya" and so forth.
Of that partless entity, with one substance...

Because that universal (sāmānya), being of the nature of a relation with what exists in that [specific] location, is of the nature of a relation with a substance such as a jar existing in a location prior to the location where the jar about to arise will be; therefore, there is no simultaneous conjunction with [a jar] in a different location. Otherwise—if it were otherwise—since there is no second self apart from that [first] self, and because that single universal is of the nature of a relation with what exists in that [specific] location, [the jar] would not be of the nature of existing in that location [where it actually arises]. Thus, "otherwise" means the absence of the nature of existing in that location.

Because of the impossibility of a connection [with multiple locations], there can be no connection at that very same time for a universal—which is by nature a single, eternal individual—with a substance located in a different place.

Or, if such a connection were to occur, since the universal would be restricted to a single essence fixed upon the previous individual, its persistence in that previous individual would simultaneously entail its non-persistence through its movement to an individual in a different place; this is a contradiction.
Thus he says: "Of a single substratum," and so forth.
In that context, "place" refers to the individual manifestation.
Because of the admission [of this], it is illogical that the universal should abide in that very same prior individual by means of that very same nature restricted to that prior individual. Why?
Because of the contradiction, in that very same prior individual, of two natures—one abiding and one non-abiding—simultaneously in a single universal.
[The phrase] "in every case" refers to the prior individual and the substance about to arise; "always" means even before the substance about to arise. ...aya... // 6 //
7 /// ... in that place there was already a commonality; therefore, what was stated—that it did not exist there—is unproven.

The meaning of "the self abiding in all forms" (*sarvākārasthitātman*) is that by whichever form the universal (*sāmānya*) existed in a previous individual, by that very same form it occurs with an identical mode of existence everywhere—even in a substance about to arise—because it is partless (*niraṃśatva*).
He refutes this with the words "of that nature" (*tatsvabhāva*), etc.:
[it is impossible] for that which has the perception of the nature of the universal as its basis to exist everywhere, even in things of a different genus (*bhinnajātīya*).
...and so forth. He asks, "For what reason?
and replies, "In a horse," and so forth.
The analysis of the compound is: that whose nature as a substance (*dravyatva*) has its self (*ātman*) abiding in a horse.
Because it conveys the meaning, a *bahuvrīhi* compound may be formed even with words in different grammatical cases;
alternatively, it is a compound formed by the rule "a noun and a *kṛt*-suffix denote the agent" (*sādhanaṃ kṛtā*), such as "standing on a horse" (*aśve sthitaḥ*).
Subsequently, a two-word *bahuvrīhi* is formed with the word *ātman*.
And because of the cognition of "substantiality" (*dravyatva*) as having the characteristics previously described, there is the cognition "it is thus, [namely] a horse.
However, this cognition "the cow is a substance" would not arise from a connection with substantiality;
for that [cognition] is indeed accepted by the opponent, but not [the cognition] "it is a horse."
For the cognition of a horse is not caused by substantiality (*dravyatva*),
but rather by horseness (*aśvatva*);
and that horseness does not exist in a cow.
Because it is admitted that the nature [of a universal] exists at all times and in all forms only within individuals of the same class.
This... ///

It is maintained that substantiality (dravyatva) exists in the object of the cognition of a horse; therefore, it must possess a property that resides in the substance which is the object of the cognition of a horse. And that substantiality, whose nature is to reside in the substance which is the object of the cognition of a horse, must exist in cows and so forth by that very same nature through which it exists in the horse.

And likewise, it would follow that even a cow would become the object of the cognition "horse"; otherwise, the nature of substanceness (*dravyatva*) would not consist in its subsistence in a substance that is the object of the cognition "horse.
Nor can one thing have two natures, by which [the former] would [apply] to a horse...

... [Even if] the mere state of being visible were seen as having the nature of subsisting in a substance that is the object of the cognition "horse," it would still not be seen; therefore, the cognition "the horse does not exist in the cow" would not arise. To this he says: "And of that... [meaning] of that universal (*sāmānya*), which is unitary and partless, there is a failure to ascertain it even though it has been grasped, due to delusion; this too is false, because it is impossible for it to function within another's perception, which consists of a determinate ascertainment (*niścaya*), as was stated previously.
The conclusion is expressed by the words "Therefore" and so forth.
[A universal] that is partless... [is not perceived].
4 /// ... does not proceed toward that; and by this much, it is explained that "it is not like a part.
He explains "it abandons the former, not the substrate" with the words beginning with "the former," etc.
"And that" refers to the abandonment of the former substrate.

The universal is not accepted as moving elsewhere; that is, while the universal remains in its previous individual (pūrvavyakti) without moving from its own former substratum-location, it would have to exist in another place where a substance has arisen from that former substratum-location. This is [the position being refuted].
5 /// ... even so, the universal would reach a substance in a different location; to this he replies with the words "where," and so forth:
in whichever location that [substance] existing at a later time resides, the universal is not connected with that location.

Because it does not admit the abandonment of its previous location, it would reach a thing existing at a later time in a place where the universal was not previously present; since this transcends logic, it is something truly marvelous—thus [the opponent] says.
6 /// ... [it is] not possible to determine [this]. Desiring also to refute the [doctrine of] omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*), he says:
"Of whom," and so forth.

Furthermore, for that proponent of a universal that is omnipresent, if the genus (*jāti*) is indeed all-pervading, then it must be manifested—made manifest by means of its manifestation, which is its individualization—in a single instance such as a brindled cow (*śābaleya*).
By that very act of being manifested, that genus would necessarily be manifested everywhere, even in places devoid of individuals and within distinct individuals of a different class.

...some particular individual (vyakti) is thus refuted... [its] occurrence is "being supported" (ādheyatā). Regarding the term "individual" (vyakti), it is not tenable in that [context], as stated in the *Itarānantara*.

Since this is so, therefore that universal (*jāti*), being by its very nature independent of the assistance of others and incapable of having any excellence added to it, would— if it were by its own nature capable of producing its own cognition—
be perceived eternally, both before and after the manifestation (*vyakti*). If, on the other hand, it is not so capable, then it would never be perceived at all.

... [of those] established by the final tenet (*siddhānta*), however, their non-existence has already been demonstrated by such statements as "simultaneously in one place" and so forth. Furthermore, those conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) arise even in the case of things perceived in dreams and the like—which are non-existent—even without a real, underlying, continuous form (*anvayirūpa*);
thus, in all cases, objects possess all aspects, yet they are strictly determined [by specific conditions].
And he states the reason for the restriction:
"only by way of distinction," and so forth;
[this applies] to those things perceived in such a manner.

4 /// ... the perception [of objects] through their differentiation, even in the case of those superimposed by one's own philosophical tenets (*siddhānta*), such as "rabbit's horn" and so forth, at the time of hearing their respective tenets;
for example, "rabbit's horn," "son of a barren woman."
At the time of acquiring proficiency in linguistic usage, because the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) for such usage is beginningless,
it is said here, etc.,
that [the object] is a single entity due to the cognition known as the "unifying reflective awareness" (*ekapratyavamarṣa*).
"Does the term 'horse' apply only to horses and the like, and not to cows and the like?
When asked this, the opponent must say exactly this: [that it applies only to horses and the like].
That is simply the power of the entity (bhāva-śakti),
by which those very things such as *dhava* trees are proximate to "treeness" (*vṛkṣatva*), whereas cows and the like are not; thus,
when the difference is equal, it is by virtue of that specific proximity.
The universal (jāti) spreads through the power of its own manifestation (bhāvaśakti) toward certain collections of objects that are intended to be its own substrata.
6 /// ...due to the power of attachment to entities; [the entity] does not, however, exist as a real substance. To this, the Sāṃkhya says:
"Not cessation," and so forth.

The "concomitance of existence" (*bhāvānvaya*) is the uniformity of the nature of things. If it were something else— that is, a real entity— then that which is the effect of one seed would not belong to another, such as the earth and so forth.
Why?
Because of the absolute difference between those two, the seed and the earth. If [it were otherwise]...

...produces [the effect]. For that which is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of that seed for producing a sprout does not belong to anything else, such as the earth and so forth. That which is superimposed by the intellect (*buddhyāropita*) and characterized by exclusion (*vyāvṛttilakṣaṇa*) is not a producer.
Why? Because exclusion, which is characterized by the negation of others, lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatvāt*).
Therefore, it is only the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the seed itself—the form (*rūpa*)—that is the producer. ...
In the *Pramāṇavārttikaṭīkā*,
[it is stated that] because a single thing characterized by the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*) lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*),
therefore only the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the seed is the productive form.
That very thing is both the object and its producer; thus, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is that which produces the sprout.
"Elsewhere" refers to [elements] such as earth and so forth.
Furthermore, [there is] the earth and so forth.

[The opponent argues: "Because of that nature of the seed which produces the sprout, the earth and so forth would be non-different from that seed. To this, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) replies with the words beginning with "If... and so on.

"Even in one [of them] is the self": that by which the causal complex is held to possess its generative power through a non-different self— that self exists even in one among those causes, within the midst of all the causes.
"...the work was accomplished by him alone."
... [the] futility of other causes.
This is not so; it is precisely at the final stage when they have come together that they possess such a capacity.

Because momentary things exist only through the presence of causes and conditions, for the other proponent who maintains eternalism, that form would always exist; thus, other causes would be rendered useless.
For this very reason it was said: "Even in a single case, that [form] exists, yet there is a difference in the sequence of causes..."

Because a single effect has a single nature, the producer [of that effect] must be non-different from those things considered to be its causes; for the productive nature remains even when only one of those causes is present.
Consequently, since the cause is never deficient in any state whatsoever, even a single entity situated anywhere would be a producer.
To reinforce this very point, he says:
"Because," and so forth: even when a single [condition], such as a seed, is present, [the effect] does not cease.
...of that [seed] which possesses the nature of producing an effect, there is a distinction from the seed in relation to the earth and so forth. What is the reason?
For if there were a distinction, the non-difference [of the cause] would be lost;
indeed, that which is intended as the producer is the non-distinct intrinsic nature (svabhāva). Since that [nature] exists even in the mere seed, [the effect would follow].
"Even though a single seed persists":
[this refers to] that undifferentiated form which is considered to be the producer.

...the distinction of states [occurs] because there is no rule for their coexistence. This has been stated while granting [the opponent's position]; otherwise, how could even specific qualities—which are distinct from other states—be destroyed by something eternal?
Furthermore, there is no distinction [in their nature], since they are not producers.
He asks, "Why is this not accepted?
and replies with the words beginning "of the auxiliary causes" (*sahakāriṇām*), etc.
Therefore, even when a single [factor] such as a seed is present...
From the state of the self of Janaka;
[regarding] "non-abiding," it refers to the singular abiding of a particularity.

If there were no [causal capacity], the production of the effect would not occur; therefore, even though the universal (*sāmānya*) remains present, when a particular (*viśeṣa*) that co-exists with it is absent, because of the lack of the fruit, the arising of that effect—from which the sprout and so forth result—occurs from the particulars, not from the universal.
That effect is the sprout and so forth.
"What is it that has become manifold? and so forth.
It means common to multiple auxiliary causes;
that is to say, produced by multiple auxiliary causes.
"Even when there is the removal of a single particularity" means:
even when there is the removal of one or another among the auxiliary causes.
8 /// ... the positive and negative concomitances (anvaya-vyatireka) of the effect pertain only to the specific [particulars], and not to the universal (sāmānya).
Thus he says:
"But not when it is incomplete."
Even when the specific distinction is present and the form is unimpaired and undifferentiated, that effect does not arise.
He analyzes this very point with the words "For the effect... and so forth.
Arising is production from something.
That very thing is the property; that which possesses it is "possessing the nature of that" (*tadbhāvadharmī*).
[This applies] even to that which at some time does not exist.
That is due to the deficiency of that progenitor;
nor is there a distinction in the nature of that which is not different from the progenitor.
When that general form (sāmānyarūpa) is unimpaired, the effect comes into being;
therefore, it indicates that the general form has the nature of non-production [of that effect].
The existence and non-existence of the effect result precisely from the existence and non-existence of the specific conditions;
and it is through the completeness or deficiency of those specific conditions that the effect comes to exist or not to exist.
Thus, there is the production of the effect.
"When that exists, it comes to be":
when a specific [cause] capable of functioning as a cause exists, the effect arises; "from something other than that" means from a generality other than that specific [cause].
Because it would lead to an over-extension:
everything would then be the cause of everything.
Since this is so, therefore only specific differences are the producers.
The universal (*sāmānya*) is not a producer;
therefore, because they are not producers, those very particulars (*viśeṣa*) are the ultimately real entities—this is the meaning.
For what reason? Because:
That is the ultimate...
He explains [the point] with the words beginning with "..."—do they explain?—as follows:
the connection is that "capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-yogyatā*) is the definition of a real entity (*vastu*), whereas incapacity is the definition of a non-entity (*avastu*).
We shall state this in the passage beginning with, "That which is capable of causal efficiency is there ultimately real (*paramārthasat*)," and so forth.
An object that is capable of performing all functions is of a specific nature;
it does not persist [as a universal],
because a specific feature does not follow after other individual instances.
That which persists is the nature of the universal;
therefore, the production of an effect is not possible from that which is of the nature of a universal.
Therefore, i...
The meaning is "in this way.
"From that very [source]" means precisely from the particularity.

... because of the production [of the effect] from that very [particular]. Thus, it has been demonstrated that the persisting form (anvayirūpa) imagined by opponents is not a producer; now, in order to refute what was stated by the opponent—that "the effect of one thing would not belong to another due to absolute difference"—he repeats that very objection.
[The author] replies with the words beginning "If [you say], 'Because there is no continuity of intrinsic nature' (*svabhāvānanvayāt*)," etc. [He states:
"In the alleviation of fever and so forth, a certain [person] together with... [and] "...one [remedy]."
That form which is the producer of one thing, such as a seed, does not exist in others, such as the earth and so forth; therefore, another [factor] would be a non-producer as a cooperative cause.

Or, if it were admitted that something possessing a nature distinct from the productive nature could be a producer, then—since there is no difference in their being distinct—all things, including barley seeds and the like, would be producers of the rice sprout.
He refutes this with the words beginning "not so" (*naitat*): [it does not follow] from a single productive rice seed.
5 /// ... [It is] not something other than the rice sprout; the word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of completing the verse, or it has the sense of the particle "eva" (only/itself).
What is the reason?

This is the nature of things: that which is the productive essence of one thing, all other things—being distinct from that very essence—would consequently become equally and simultaneously productive, because there is no difference in their distinction [from it].
Or rather, there is no creator at all;
this objection might arise if [the self] were produced from one of these.
...just as [it was said] before. "From that" means:

even though there is no difference in the distinction of the specific [causes], [the effect arises] from some particular excellence of the self (ātma-atiśaya), characterized by its determination toward a specific result.
A certain thing, such as the earth and so forth, is the producer of a rice sprout, and not another, such as a barley seed and so forth. Why is this?
The specific capacity of that [earth and so forth] to produce a rice sprout is its nature as a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*), and not that of another, such as a barley seed;
this alone constitutes the distinction.
What was done...?
...it would not be logical.
For what reason? Because this aforementioned intrinsic nature [must have a cause].
Indeed, there must necessarily be a cause for a distinction in intrinsic nature.

Because, if it were causeless, there would be no restriction regarding place and so forth since it would not depend on a cause, which would lead to the over-extension [of the consequence] that things would exist everywhere, at all times, and in their entirety. Therefore, it is said that its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) arises from its own cause, which is regarded as its cause.
Of that...
...the beginningless succession of causes is not a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the distinction of causes for distinct entities. He says "distinct," etc., to express this very point.
Because of the nature of things (*vastusthiti*), [causes are distinct]; however, he states that there is a subverting proof against their being one.
"But if there is no difference," and so forth:
because of their mutual non-difference, upon the destruction of one, there would be the simultaneous destruction of all—
this is from the *Pramāṇavārttikaṭīkā*.
Because there is no distinction by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), [the following would not occur]:
"arising through differentiation" and so forth;
that is, the arising of one and the non-arising of another, the persistence of one and the cessation of another—thus, arising and the rest could not exist as distinct entities.
But rather, they [the properties] should occur only once, as in the case of one's own self (*svātman*).

Just as for a single particular state there is no production and so forth through differentiation, so too [is it here]. Positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is the defining characteristic of that non-difference, even though [the entity] exists.
"...ityādi.
In the Sūtra, however, the mention of "arising from non-existence" (*abhavagrahaṇa*) is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an indicative mark).

For, by means of that very [mark]—namely, arising without distinction and so forth—the absence of difference is ascertained through indication; otherwise, by what would difference and non-difference be indicated?

"Even for that which has a single form" means even for that which has an identical form; "separation" (*vyatireka*) consists in having a distinct origination and so forth, and that is the definition of difference.
Having an undivided origination and so forth is "non-separation" (*avyatireka*), and that is the definition of non-difference.
3 /// ... because of the contradiction between the pair [of properties] such as arising and non-arising.
It is not the case that objects are entirely without distinction; rather, there is also distinction.
For that reason...
If it is argued that this is not so, because there is no consequence of [the mind] arising all at once and so forth, he says:
"No," and so on; this is the explanation of that very point.
Indeed, we do not assert that there is no distinction or non-difference in every respect—
which would entail such consequences as simultaneous destruction and arising— [but rather only in certain respects].
... characterized by [these] marks, distinct, and consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇya*), because the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion is without distinction everywhere.
Thus, it differs from the aforementioned characteristics of states.
If that is so, then because the universal (*sāmānya*) is eternal, it must abide everywhere.
But the destruction of the particulars is accepted; therefore, when one particular is perishing,
that which remains as the nature of the universal cannot be the [cause] of that particular.

5 /// ... otherwise, if it were admitted that "place" (*sthāna*) and "non-place" (*asthāna*) have a single substratum, then two contradictory properties would be accepted within a single self. And if that were so, what other property could serve as a differentiator? None at all. Indeed, two contradictory properties are not accepted in one and the same place;
for specific qualities (*viśeṣa*), by virtue of their distinct arising and so forth, are differentiated in every respect.
But because there is no separate arising and so forth for the universal (*sāmānya*), it is non-discriminative with respect to everything; therefore, he says:
"In all aspects," etc., meaning it is both discriminative and non-discriminative in all aspects.
6 /// ... [When] difference and generality are distinct, this mere designation would not be accepted;
however, the entity itself is not rejected.
Indeed, an entity consisting of both difference and generality is precisely accepted as being mutually distinct.
And this was stated previously,
by means of the passage beginning with "or because one accepts another name for the object and designates it accordingly.
"Tat" means "therefore."
"These entities"—
whether they be particulars or universals—
are indeed mutually distinct.
Of what nature is it? It is one that does not share the same security and well-being.
For that reason,
there would be no cognition of the universal and the particular;
the meaning is that there would be no cognition characterized by a mutual relationship between the universal and the particular.

And because of the absence of cognition (*buddhi*), even designation (*vyapadeśa*) is indeed refuted. Since the absence of designation has been stated [in the verse], it follows as a necessary concomitant that there is an absence of cognition; thus, the absence of cognition is also effectively stated by implication (*arthāt*).
Therefore, this universal is a distinct entity from the particulars;
it is not dependent upon the particulars.
Why? Because that universal is not produced by those particulars.
The second meaning is this: the entity consisting of particularity (*bheda*); it is a different object from the universal (*sāmānya*), and within that [particular], the universal...

... [one] would apply the designation "this is the universal of this particular" or "this particular belongs to this universal. This same undesirable consequence follows even if the universal is defined as the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).
When one [tree] perishes,
[the notion] "the self remains" and so forth arises;
for instance, when a *dhava* or a *khadira* tree perishes.
"The exclusion of non-trees certainly remains in other trees.
He refutes this with the words "no," and so forth.
The meaning here is as follows: for the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) is threefold.
First, one... [text fragment]

... because it is excluded from both intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and extrinsic nature (*parabhāva*). Furthermore, it is established as the basis for conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) that relies upon words and logical marks (*liṅga*), but not by way of being denotable by words.
The second [type of exclusion] is merely the exclusion of others (*anyavyavacchedamātra*).

It is on the basis of "exclusion of others" (*anyāpohana*) being [defined as] "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) that this [universal] is established by the former teachers as being non-differentiated everywhere; for a mere negation would be subject to all [the aforementioned faults].
conceptual construction...
...is intended as that which is denotable by words. Regarding that [which is] excluded from others, it is said with reference to the particular (svalakṣaṇa).
That is incorrect;
for that which constitutes the very essence of its object must necessarily perish when that object perishes, due to their non-difference.
And as for that other specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which remains, it is indeed admitted to be distinct from it.
And since that which is a mere negation lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), this objection does not apply;
thus it is said:
"Because exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) lacks intrinsic nature."
Neither established nor unestablished...

Thus, this [treatment] of what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna*) belongs to that very exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). Furthermore, those characteristics of the forms of conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhyākāralakṣaṇa*) which consist in the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*), as well as that which is an error (*upaplava*) and a delusion (*vibhrama*), do not follow the nature of real entities (*vastvanupātin*).

Therefore, even for the conceptualizing cognition of a universal (*sāmānyadhiyo vikalpikāyā buddheḥ*), that [exclusion] does not exist at all externally. Precisely because it is thus a distortion (*viplavatva*), for that reason, that exclusion is not a fault.
... [How] is it precisely false knowledge? If one asks this, he says:

"That which," and so forth. Because in a single instance there is neither stability nor instability of that universal (*sāmānya*)—which is the object of the conceptualizing consciousness (*vikalpavijñāna*)—since that object of false knowledge does not exist.
Having removed the charge of parity of fault, the objection previously raised is pursued again by way of another method.

K. *Pramāṇavārttikaṭīkā* r1 /// ... the existence [of the capacity]; and as for that form of the rice seed which produces the rice sprout, how could earth and the other elements—which are distinct from that productive form—be producers?
To this, introduced by "therein" (*tatra*) or in response to that objection, it is replied: [...]
We do not say that for something other than the rice seed, such as the earth and so forth, there is no nature that produces it—that is, no nature that produces the sprout.
What then? [That which belongs to one...]
"...not in the form of a rice seed. Why? Because it is not that [same thing], because it does not have that intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

And he says, "they, each according to its own [nature]," and so forth, meaning those elements such as earth and the rest; for there is no subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) here [to contradict this].

"According to their own [nature]" (*yathāsvam*) means that whatever is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of each thing, by that they are mutually distinct; yet, by their very nature (*svabhāvena*), they are established as producers of a single effect. What contradiction is there in this? None at all, because there is no subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*). [This is so] by way of the actual state of things (*vastusthiti*), but not by way of the form of a rice seed which is considered the producer of a rice sprout. It is not contradictory for earth and other factors—though lacking that specific form of the rice seed—to have the rice sprout as their effect. To this, he says:
One...
3 /// ... it would not have the nature of being a seed of that [rice]; rather, it must be its effect. The analysis of the compound is: "that rice-sprout is the effect of this."
If, however, the seed alone were the producer of the sprout, there would be a contradiction; but that is not the case.
Thus he says, "by that very [seed]," and so forth.
"By that very" means by the rice seed itself.
With the words "that effect called the sprout," and so forth, he recalls what was stated previously:
"Because in the absence of even one [of the causes] there is no fruit, its production arises from the specific [causes]."
4 /// ... not by way of its specific form (*rūpa*).
That which is the producer of one seed does not exist in others such as the earth; therefore, they are not so [capable].
Even though the earth and other factors are non-different [from the seed], they are non-producers merely due to the deficiency of the form of the seed, and so forth.
The meaning is that even within those distinctions, there is non-difference.

He explains this with the words "It might be so," and so forth; [the phrase] "not, however, of them" refers to the particulars (*viśeṣa*), because that very undivided form is joined with a single capacity.
By the word "thereby," the Teacher [refers to that].
By that undifferentiated form, those particularities [are established].
...the particularities [are not destroyed], because that universal form is eternal and never departs.
(In the margin: //
In that form which is their common nature, those particulars are the producers [of the effect].

Why? Because that common nature is eternal and does not perish; for if the cause were to remain as a single entity, it would follow that the effect must be produced [at all times]. Moreover, this undifferentiated form does not perish, whereas the particulars indeed do perish.
By the passage beginning with "ityādinā," what was stated previously— namely, that destruction and arising would occur simultaneously— would have been established.

Having proven their difference through the imposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) by means of the passage beginning with "nāśotpādau sakṛd," he says "kiñca" and so forth in order to prove it also by means of a difference in appearance (*pratibhāsabheda*).
What is the specific characteristic of the appearance? It is that which does not partake of anything else and is distinct from conceptual construction.
"...is liberated. For him, the proponent of non-differentiation (*abhedavādin*), there is a differentiation of the appearance in cognition (*buddhipratibhāsabheda*);
that is, a differentiation of the forms (*ākāra*) of cognition, and [a differentiation] such as arising and perishing separately."

Or, if that difference in appearance and so forth were admitted while there is no difference among entities, then nothing would ever function as a differentiator—even in the case of pleasure, pain, delusion, and consciousness.
And thus, if there is no difference, this distinction—namely, the distinction of appearance and so forth—would be like a single essence; just as in a single pleasure, [there is no...]
The internal distinction is indeed a specific difference, being entirely distinct from one another. Of what nature is it? It is characterized by distinct appearances and so forth;
it is distinct.
The analysis of the compound is: "that which has an appearance and so forth.
If it is argued that because there is an appearance here, even though it is non-different [from the object], there is therefore also non-difference [between them], he says:
"And not here," and so forth.
"Here" refers to among the particulars;
"by the power of that" means by the power of the non-differentiated appearance.
Therefore, it is precisely a distinction, indeed a difference;
it is not non-difference either.
That very distinction is the object, the real entity.
However, as for those other general properties such as "treeness" and so forth, they are merely conceptualized exclusions (vyāvṛtti) of that very [particular];
thus it says "its effect" and so on.
The word "effect" (*kārya*) and so on is neuter because it does not stand in grammatical coreferentiality (*asamānādhikaraṇya*).
Otherwise, since a particular (*viśeṣa*) has been introduced [as the subject], it would have to be "that" (*sa*).

That very form of the particular is called both the effect and the cause; that very thing is called the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), and the phrase "having as its fruit the abandonment and attainment of that" refers to that very particular which is to be abandoned or to be adopted.

Those active processes for which there is a fruit are so described; and that [fruit], which performs a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), belongs only to that particularity (*viśeṣa*). Thus, the difference of the particularity from another of a different class is a mere exclusion (*vyāvṛtti-mātra*), and not some real entity called a "universal" (*sāmānya*).
If such a universal were to exist, it would have to meet the conditions for perception (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*).

It would be perceived apart from its particularity; for, since that universal possesses the nature of an object and the nature of a real entity, there can be no non-perception of the form of that which exists as something visible, nor a failure to grasp its own intrinsic nature.

3 /// ... [regarding] the notion of non-difference among those [things], for [non-difference] itself is not a cause for apprehending another [thing]. Just as for the Sāṃkhya, despite the lack of distinction in non-difference, not everything is the means for producing everything, so too for the Buddhist, despite the lack of distinction in difference. To which objection, then, does this resolution apply? He says: "As for what was stated," and so forth.
"Because it has the nature of producing that" means because it has the nature of producing a rice sprout;
[the earth and other elements] are distinct from it.
How could this [seed] be the producer of this sprout? Or, if its status as a producer were being established, there would be a distinction...
This is called the second [point]. What, then, is it here?
It begins with "yadi" (if), etc.:

even though the difference is equal, if there were no specific distinction in that [difference] characterized by being a producer or a non-producer of a restricted effect, [then the following would occur].
"This might be the objection," [he says].
He states the meaning of the verse with the words "Just as... and so forth.
The connection is: "In the same way, even though there is a distinction, not everything will be the producer of everything."

Regarding the phrase "by way of the nature of things" (*vastudharmatayā*): if the non-difference of entities is accepted on the basis of the power of things (*vastuśaktyā*), then [the consequence would be] that... [of that... //
He explains [the verse] beginning with "In the third... and so forth:

the cause (*hetu*) is the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*), while the conditions (*pratyaya*) are the cooperative causes (*sahakārin*). "Their own causes and conditions" (*svahetupratyaya*) refers to those very causes and conditions; that which is determined by them is capable of producing a specific effect.

Those for whom an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) has been established are referred to as such; their state is that [intrinsic nature]. Therefore, "not other" means that things other than what is intended to be a non-agent would not be agents. For what reason? Because they lack that intrinsic nature;
because they lack the intrinsic nature of producing that particular effect.
"Of that" means of that single triad of qualities; "in that very place" means in one and the same effect; "thus" means not indeed by way of being non-different...

Furthermore, if [it were the case that] the rice seed and the barley seed [were identical], then in one and the same thing, both activity and non-activity would follow as consequences. Yet, even for that which possesses the three qualities (*triguṇya*), there is a difference due to its respective configuration (*sanniveśa*).
Therefore, if it is argued that because of this difference some things lack activity, [the response is] "no," and so forth, as a refutation.
If difference were the cause for non-action, you would not produce auxiliary causes because they too are mutually different.
He explains [this] with the words "no," etc., [asking]: "Why [is there] non-distinction in all aspects and absolute identity, even though there is difference?"
7 /// ... because of the distinction between states. Otherwise, even for the Sāṃkhya who professes reality (*tattva*), non-difference would be difficult to establish.
(L) *Pramāṇavārttikaṭīkā*

... [because] due to the utilization of everything, there is simply no state of being a non-agent; therefore, he says: "by way of a turn" (*paryāyeṇa*). What is the meaning of that? Is it not the case that this turn belongs to that very same single entity? Such is the sense.
The meaning is that this is because a synonym (*paryāya*) has difference as its basis.
He explains this with the words "Now" (*atha*) and so forth:
because all differences are employed in every effect sequentially, that is, in succession.
And this occurs when the power of the *pradhāna*...

...only the primary power (*pradhāna-śakti*) itself is the real entity (*vastu-sat*); it alone is employed in purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). Differences (*bheda*), however, are merely causes for conventional designation; in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), they do not exist at all.
This is stated as follows:
"Or of power," and so forth.

[This refers to] that which is characterized by the three qualities (*traiguṇya*), which is inherent in it, which was previously inherent in an entity considered not to be an agent, and which subsequently undergoes transformation into another form—that is, into the form of what is considered an agent.
... [it is] so called because of that which exists for it. How could it not be so for a single [entity]?
By this, the question "Is it of that very same entity? has been explained. Or, as it was stated: "or of the capacity."
Regarding this, he says: "Or else, it is transformation.
How can there be a diminution or the attainment of another state for a power that is non-different from its previous distinct state?
If a distinction from its prior state is admitted for the triple nature (traiguṇya) after [that change], then, because of that distinction... [the rest of the sentence is missing].

...will be [asserted]. And since there would be mutual [identity] between difference and generality, this being the case, in a real entity (*vastu*) that possesses both generality and particularity, there would be absolute difference and non-difference.
Because the generality is not distinct from the particulars, its form is different; thus, there is absolute difference due to the absence of generality.
Because the particulars are not distinct from the generality, they are one; thus, there is absolute non-difference.
Because there is an absolute absence of particularities, [the universal] is one; it is the commonality of distinctions.

5 /// ... If [it is argued that] there is a connection between the similar and dissimilar selves—that is, between the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*)—[then] they would possess that [universal] by means of a non-different self called *pradhāna*, which constitutes their very essence;
they would thus possess a non-different nature.

That differentiation whose nature is non-different from the self called "Pradhāna" is one that has a non-differentiated nature; because of that state, how could there even be differentiation for that [Pradhāna]?
There is no mutual differentiation at all by this [reasoning].

The self does not exist as a single entity because it possesses a manifold nature. Since it exists through both a universal nature and a particular nature, it is not logical for it to exist as a universal nature alone; for the universal is not distinct from the particular. The meaning is that there is no such thing as "sameness" [if it were not differentiated].
By this, absolute difference is explained;
for if it were so—as when the *pradhāna* is held to have the nature of a universal—the *pradhāna* itself would not possess those properties, namely, the properties of non-difference.
[The text is: *avya...*
The meaning is that [the state] would not exist;
that is to say, there would be a mutual difference between the state and that which possesses the state. Establishing this very point, he says:
"For this," and so forth.
The connection is as follows: "It is not logical that this [entity], which possesses a single intrinsic nature, should possess both activity and cessation."
Abiding is activity; departure is cessation. For it is accepted that when power is established, there is the cessation of states.
By this, [the argument] that "there is a mutual difference between those two," and so forth, has been explained.
With the words "no" (*na*) and so on, he anticipates the opponent's intention regarding the universal (*sāmānya*).

8 /// ... however, if there were a distinction even between those two—distinction and generality—then for this Sāṃkhya, whether in the case of a particular or a universal, there would be no absolute distinction or non-distinction; such is the connection [of the words].

Since the opponent maintains the doctrine of oneness (*ekatva*), it is understood that absolute distinction does not exist; but how is it that non-distinction is not absolute? To this, he states the reason:
"By means of distinction," and so forth.
Because [the universal] is established as distinct [from the particulars]— the universal being the power (*śakti*) and the manifestations being the particulars (*viśeṣa*)—
[it is said] "by which," and so forth.

Regarding the statement, "The universal is that by which [the particular] is established as such": if there is a difference between the universal and the particular by means of that very nature, then there is an absolute difference. He explains this with the words "if" and so forth.
The phrase "that nature" refers to the nature consisting of capacity (*śakti*) and manifestation (*vyakti*).
The grammatical connection is: "if there is a difference between the universal and the particular by means of that nature."
Clarifying this very point, he says "yasmāt" and so forth:
for those two selves which establish the distinction [between the two] belong to them; thus [it refers to] the common [property].
If those two [states] were distinct—that is, mutually different—then their distinction would be nothing other than difference itself.
Why? Because of the difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
It might be thought: "It is only the entity (*bhāva*) that establishes the distinction between the state and the possessor of the state that differs, not the intrinsic nature. To this, he says:
"Self-nature indeed," and so forth.
The meaning is that self-nature (*svabhāva*) is itself the entity (*bhāva*).

"And likewise" refers to the two—the particular and the universal (or the universal and the particular)—which are their own selves, being constituted by their self-nature; if those two were distinct from one another...

...the very distinction [between the two states]. What is the reason? Because of the difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). It might be thought that it is the entity (*bhāva*) itself—which establishes the distinction between the two states—that differs, and not the intrinsic nature. To this he says: "When there is absolute difference, there would be a lack of generality for the distinction and a lack of particularity for the universal"—this is the connection [of the sentence].
The meaning is that the universal would not possess differentiation, nor would differentiations possess the universal, because such a thing is impossible;
just as, for example, because there is no relation between differentiated things such as pots and so forth, they do not possess one another mutually.

"...because there is no connection by way of being produced [from it], it was said [in the intermediate passage]: 'therefore, the cognition of a universal as distinct [from the particular] would not occur.
Alternatively, this effort made by others is misplaced; for they imagine a universal that is distinct from the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)."

Or rather, is it not so? For that [permanent entity] is asserted by others to be eternal; consequently, because it cannot perform a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), it is like the horn of a hare. Therefore, for one who seeks purposeful action, the investigation into difference and non-difference is irrelevant.
... [except] otherwise, in order to demonstrate the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of that which is conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*), he says "And also," and so forth.

Having placed before him—that is, having made the object of his focus—that self (*ātman*) which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-yogya*), this person proceeds, desiring the fruit to be accomplished by it; that is, he possesses the longing for the fruit to be accomplished by means of that self. This is the person who engages [in action].
Difference and non-difference are considered as having that [entity] as their basis and that as their substratum;
and of that [entity], which is capable of causal efficiency, its own...

...in accordance with the appearance of limited intellect, there is indeed a determination of that state [of identity] once the task has been accomplished; it is for this reason alone that those seeking purposeful action engage in the consideration of difference and non-difference.
Therefore, as for the universal (*sāmānya*), which does not perform any purposeful action, what is the use of considering its difference or non-difference from the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)?

"Let the real entity itself be the universal; what is the use of an imagined exclusion (vyāvṛtti)? To this he says: "The real entity does not persist," because particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) do not [persist] among one another...
... [it is] established. Regarding that, he says "arising and so forth," and so on.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), there is the implication of [the faults of] simultaneous arising, cessation, and so on.
He explains this with the words "all indeed," and so forth.

The meaning is that it is precisely the particularity (*viśeṣa*), which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāyogya*), called "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*), and which constitutes the very essence (*ātmabhūta*).
With reference to what entity (*bhāva*) or thing (*vastu*) does [the cognition] proceed?

"That very thing" refers to the particular (viśeṣa) which performs causal efficiency (arthakriyākārī). "In that way" means that those seeking causal efficiency [engage] with the unique particular (svalakṣaṇa) by means of words such as "cow" and so forth.

... [it is] precisely in that way that [the object] is determined. Therefore, this was stated with regard to the function of words based on the force of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of those who employ linguistic conventions.

However, since there is no manifestation of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) in verbal cognition, it is stated that the particular characteristic is inexpressible; thus, there is no contradiction.

However, "substantiality" and so forth [are mentioned] therein; that is, when there is an injunction regarding a cow or the like by means of words such as "cow," why is it that they—namely substantiality and so forth—are denoted separately from the substance by their respective words for substantiality and so on?

M Pramāṇavārttikaṭīkā r1 /// ... and so forth. Because the object, such as a cow, is not deviant from its universal, such as "cowness," there would be a cognition of universals from that object; however, a word denoting a particular does not operate upon a universal. And this has been thoroughly examined by the Teacher Diṅnāga in the *Sāmānyaparīkṣā* and other works, regarding how words for particulars [do not apply to universals].
"There is no occurrence in the universal.
To this, it is objected: "The universal... [text fragment].
That too is exactly so.
Likewise, there is no non-deviation of the appearance in conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) from an external substance, because that [appearance] is independent.

It is said: the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself, when excluded from its own class (*sajātīya*), is the "particular" (*viśeṣa*); that very same thing, when taken without distinction with respect to its exclusion from other classes (*vijātīya*), is called the "universal" (*sāmānya*).
Therefore, because the universal and the particular are in reality one, [the effect is] produced...
However, due to the distinction [in the means of cognition], it is said that in some cases there is verbal comprehension (*śābdī pratipatti*) and in others there is objective comprehension (*ārthī*).
"That" (*tad*) means for this reason; "this person" (*ayaṃ puruṣaḥ*).

That which is presented as a cow and so forth, brought together by the word "cow" and so forth, and which is the locus of causal efficiency— [the cognition] of which has two faces because it presents another entity, namely the universal, in the form of both the particular and the universal, is described as such.
That which is the self or intrinsic nature of this cow and so forth, which is not shared with other portions [of reality].
Regarding the phrase "having placed before him that object which possesses such-and-such efficacy," the object (*ālambana*) is intended.
One who desires a specific purposeful action speaks of that very [object] with the words "just as," and so forth.
Just as one who desires the carrying of a load or the milking of a cow proceeds by placing the cow itself before him.

The meaning of the sentence "of that which occurs elsewhere" (*anyasaṃbhavinaḥ*) is as follows: a person desiring an object that occurs in something other than a cow—namely, in a horse—does not act by taking the cow as the primary objective. To explain what kind of object occurs elsewhere, he says: "Just as in the case of [the word] *yuddha*... and so forth.

... [it is] understood as such. By the transformation of the case ending (*vibhaktivipariṇāmena*), the connection is with "by the injunction (*codanayā*) of the distinctions of cows and so forth" (*gavādīnāṃ bhedānām*). And by the injunction of the words "cow" and so forth, it means "at that time. Because at the time of activity for one desiring an action, the generality (*sāmānya*) of substance and so forth is not intended to be attained; thus is the connection through the transformation of the case ending. It is true that specific individuals (*viśeṣa*) such as cows and so forth are enjoined by those desiring purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), but those are the distinctions of substance (*dravya*).
To this he says:
"Because of the inclusion [of the universal] in the cow and so forth.

For the Sāṃkhya, who maintains that there is no difference [between the universal and the particular], this means that because the universal is included in the particulars such as cows—entering into them through identity—it follows that [the universal] has the nature of the cow and so forth.

If it is argued that the nature of being distinct is indeed accepted for universals, he says: "And [of those] which have become their very self," meaning of the universals whose intrinsic nature is that of cows and so forth.
