[The text continues: "Like cows and so forth..."
... because it has precisely that as its nature, just as [it was said] before.
And therefore, it is specifically the particularity (viśeṣa) that is questioned; he says "that very one" and so forth.
A person seeking purposeful action (arthakriyā) interrogates that very entity, which is not shared by anything else, by means of various modes of difference and non-difference.

Even for the proponent of *anyāpoha*, the non-difference of "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and so forth, characterized by exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), is accepted as being from the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*); therefore, absolute difference among particulars is contradictory.

The non-difference of this [universal] from [particulars] such as "being existent" (sat-tva) and so forth is not at all a subverter [of difference], because that [non-difference] is merely imagined. Therefore, the difference of ultimate particularities (svalakṣaṇa) is real, while their unity is conceptualized. And since difference and non-difference are accepted by us in this manner, he says the following to demonstrate precisely that:
"Everywhere," and so forth;
the connection is that this is because one accepts that the universal (*sāmānya*) is characterized by exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).
It is not [perceived] as a universal in the form of exclusion...

It has been stated [previously] that because of their commonality and lack of distinction, there is either an identity of particulars like the particulars themselves, or else a multiplicity of the universal. It was not said there that particulars possess identity by accepting a universal;
rather, he says that the non-difference [of particulars] is due to that very particularity itself.
"By its own self," and so forth: if cows, horses, and the like were non-different by their very own specific forms (*viśeṣarūpa*), then that substance... [ni] //
"Of two" means of both the cow and the horse.

For even a single object denoted by the word "cow," when intended as a cause, performs that specific purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) consisting of carrying and yielding milk because it possesses that nature;
it performs it precisely because its nature is to perform that purposeful action.
"Of another as well": therefore, even for another [entity] than that cow-substance—such as a horse—that [utility], such as carrying or milking... [is absent].
N. *Pramāṇavārttikaṭīkā* r1 /// ... [the] distinction of ... not being shameless by way of nakedness;
[he is] devoid of modesty, a destroyer, because the improper statement is laughable; he says "something" (kim api).
That which they prattle—namely, that everything has the nature of all things and yet does not have the nature of all things—is also refuted.

Why? Because of the possibility of a single extreme; for there exists one extreme consisting of an absolutely distinct mode [of being]. Thus, because of the identity of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of curd, it might be a camel; yet because of the difference in state, it might not be curd. This is improper (*aślīla*).
Thus, this explanation is incorrect.
Because "aślīla" is a synonym for "vulgar," [the phrase] "neither to be rejected nor to be accepted" means that which is neither to be abandoned nor to be grasped.
Why? Because there is no finality.
For if some means of happiness were established as such, while another were [established as] suffering...
Because it does not have the nature of all things, nor because it has the nature of everything;
and for this reason, it is undifferentiated, since it is impossible to grasp a single extreme.

Or, if there were a succession of that distinction of natures, or a succession of one after another, then everything would possess both forms, and there would be the grasping of both. When that exists, it is the indication of multiplicity.

Because there is the negation of such a specific characteristic— namely, that a camel is only a camel and not curd, and that curd is only curd and not a camel— the [injunction] "Eat the curd" [is established].
3 /// ... by virtue of its own nature, there would be curd;

nor is it the case that the camel itself is exclusively the camel—this being an extremist view—by which another thing such as curd would also be a camel, for in that case curd too would be a camel. Nor is it the case that that very curd is exclusively curd, by which another thing such as a camel would also be curd. By this, [the opponent attempts to establish] the dual nature of everything...
It has been explained.
He explains that [statement], namely "because of the exclusion of its particularity" (*tadviśeṣanirākṛteḥ*), with the words "of those two" (*tad anayoḥ*) and so forth.
For in both ways, there would indeed be a particularity (*viśeṣaḥ*).
...then it would necessarily be of the very nature of a camel.
The same should be said for curd as well.

First, the impossibility of the former [curd] is explained by the words "that" and so forth; thus, the connection is that there is no distinction whatsoever between these two, namely curd and the camel.
Regarding the phrase "even of one": because there is an absence of that form—namely, the absence of the form of a camel (*uṣṭra*) or the absence of the form of curd (*dadhi*)—in either case;
he states the absence of the second mode as well with the words "of its own nature" (*svarūpasya*), and so forth.
Because there is no such thing as a camel that is fixed in its nature as a camel, nor anything fixed in its nature as curd. Now,
if there were some excellence (*atiśaya*) in curd and the camel by virtue of which a person, when urged to "eat curd," would act with distinction— namely,
proceeding toward the curd alone while avoiding the camel— [then that excellence would exist].

That very excellence is the curd, and that [excellence] does not exist elsewhere in the camel; thus every entity, whose nature is differentiated as neither one nor the other, is the ultimate reality (paramārtha), whereas unity is merely...
... [in the] explanation ... thus, regarding curd and milk: "Thus instructed" means that a person who is instructed, "Eat the curd," proceeds by way of distinction;
he proceeds toward the curd itself, excluding the camel.

That very excellence (*atiśaya*) is the curd; it does not exist elsewhere, such as in the camel. Therefore, every entity whose nature is differentiated from both [its causes and other things] is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); oneness, however, is merely imagined.
The phrase "another [object], such as a camel, which is of the nature of experience, by means of curd itself" is to be explained in this manner.
7 /// "Prompted" means one who is prompted [to think] "eat curd.
Curd is a modification of milk and nothing else; thus, it exists in the camel.

That very excellence which is curd is the object of the activity of a person seeking purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). It is the object of the activity of that person who seeks the purposeful action to be accomplished by curd. For what reason? Because it bears that fruit, and so forth.
The analysis of the compound is as follows: because it is accomplished by curd itself, it is a "specific result" (*phalaviśeṣa*); and that very thing is the "specificity" (*viśeṣa*).

Its state of being the material cause (*upādānabhāva*) is its state of being the cause (*hetubhāva*); the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a given entity which is characterized by that [state] is what is meant by "that very thing" (*tad eva*).
The nature of curd [is not found] elsewhere— that is, in a camel. Why?
Because one who desires curd has no inclination toward a camel in that context,
the two [terms] have restricted meanings:
the words *dhī* and *dhvani* refer respectively to cognition and sound.
Because of the absence of that [intrinsic nature], and because of the existence of distinct cognitions and words for those differences,
the doctrine of the synthesis of differences and the doctrine of unification are impossible.
A "specification" (*nirdeśa*) would be the subsumption as one of two things that have been perceived or heard separately, such as "the camel is the curd.
He explains this with the words "this is that," and so forth. Where? [The answer follows: "In the case of... etc.
The connection [of the sentence] is: "Not perceiving the aspect (ākāra), how could one be convinced of the objects by means of the intellect?
To the question "By what kind of intellect?", he says: "unmixed," and so forth.
That [intellect] which has as its object that which is thus described is called such.
That cognition of which he possesses [the awareness] is one that is unmixed, possessing other forms, and grasping distinct objects—this is what is meant.
Or rather, how could he express it by means of a sound through a specific convention? This is the intended meaning.
He asks: "Why would one not be convinced? and says:

"Because there is no division of entities"—this is the doctrine of their dissolution. There would be no doctrine of the dissolution of distinctions, such as [the statement] "it is a camel," and so forth. Furthermore, having perceived the curd and the camel as unmixed, [one then perceives their] dissolution...

Because of the restriction [of cognition] in some cases to a camel and in others to curd—by means of a non-composite cognition that grasps a non-composite form, even though it is associated with a composite [object] such as a camel or curd—the difference in nature between those two forms, curd and camel, is caused solely by the difference in the appearance of the cognition;
that is, it is caused solely by the difference in the appearance of the cognition.
Why?

Regarding the passage beginning with "one or many" (*ekāneka*), it should be understood as follows: the establishment of multiplicity is the object of a difference in appearance (*pratibhāsabheda*), while the establishment of unity is the object of a non-difference in appearance.
[The phrase] "distinct appearance" (*bhinnapratibhāsa*)... [is to be supplied].
... thus, it is not that [the object] is both a camel and curd; rather, the analysis of the compound is "that which has the nature consisting of both curd and camel.
Syādvāda would then be nothing but false speech (*mithyāvāda*).
"The characteristic of distinction" means the characteristic of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), by its very nature... [svabhāvena].
The distinction between the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of things that possess designations is exclusion from others by means of their very intrinsic nature.
"Therein" refers to those things that lack any designation (*nirupākhya*).

Furthermore, it cannot be maintained by the proponent of *anyāpoha* (exclusion of others) that words do not function with respect to things that are non-existent (*nirupākhya*). This is because words must necessarily function even with respect to those [non-existent things], for some reason or other;
otherwise, since they are not established as objects of cognition or words, injunctions and prohibitions would be impossible in the case of every object whatsoever.
If, in some case, cognition and verbal designation were to occur through the negation of an unreal form, then [they would apply] to an object that excludes the negated form...
5 /// ... the two [types of] affirmation and negation.
That conventional usage (vyavahāra) which has such a basis is described as "that.
He explains that very absence of conventional usage with the words beginning with "camel" (uṣṭra).
The conventional usage "fire has heat as its intrinsic nature" is based on positive concomitance (*anvaya*);

"it is not non-hot" is based on negative exclusion (*vyatireka*). By the word "also" (*api*), he indicates that even this highly renowned worldly convention would not exist [without such a basis]. For the determination of "hot" occurs through the exclusion of "non-hot."
And for that which is not hot, there is the absence of heat.
6 /// ... it might be asked; therefore he says "by another intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvāntara*) and so forth.

The absence of heat itself is "another" (*antara*), meaning distinct (*vilakṣaṇa*) from the intrinsic nature of heat, insofar as it consists in the negation of that [nature]. Thus, it is called "another intrinsic nature.
For this very reason, the statement "of that which is non-existent" (*asataḥ*) is appropriate.
But a particular intrinsic nature is not a different intrinsic nature,
because it can in no way be established as the object of conceptual cognition or of a word.
7 /// ... [If] the nature of fire were such that it were the same for every entity, then the world would be deluded and of an indeterminate form.

It might be argued: "In that case, there is no negation of anything non-existent regarding fire and so forth, such that there must necessarily be the occurrence of a word even in the absence [of the object]. To this we reply: rather, it is a real thing called touch, which is not hot and is indeed a distinct entity from fire, that is being negated.
Fire is hot, not non-hot;
because there is a negation such as "there is no non-hot touch in fire," how [could it be otherwise]? And so forth.
From the statement "Being indeed," there is existence.
[He] brings it forth: by the statement "there is no non-heat in fire," we do not mean that heat is non-existent everywhere.
For if it were stated in that way, having first asserted existence and then subsequently denying existence everywhere, one would be asserting both existence and non-existence in the same place.
Rather, we simply say that in that specific case—namely, in fire—non-heat does not exist.
Furthermore, the non-existence of that which exists in one place in another place is not contradictory;
and this very principle is what [the author] states with the words beginning "deśa" (place), etc., [in the passage]: "iha nā... and so forth.

O *Pramāṇavārttikaṭīkā*: Why is there no negation of the subject (*dharmin*)? Because if that [subject] were negated—that is, if the subject were negated—the word whose object it is would have no object and thus could not function; consequently, since the word for the subject would not function, the negative particle (*nañ*) would have no designated object.

Because that [object] is not employed [in the cognition], the object of negation must necessarily be presented by the initial words [of the sentence] as "this is not here"; otherwise, it would not be known what the object of this negation is.
"Also here" means by the negation of place, time, and the property (*dharma*), the inclusion of "place" and so forth—whereby "and so forth" includes time—is intended.

The plural number is used because of the distinction between individual instances (*vyakti*), not because of a plurality of the object (*artha*) itself; that is, it is not the substratum (*dharmin*) that is indicated by the word "object.
This is because even the opponent does not desire the negation of the substratum.
The subject (*dharmin*) is not the rabbit’s horn and so forth,
nor is the location and so forth being negated; rather,
in the statement "the rabbit’s horn does not exist," there is a [negation] of the relation between the rabbit and the horn.
...also because there is no negation [of it].

He establishes that very point with the words "if it were non-existent" (*asati*) and so forth: if there were no connection, there would be no application of the word; for the negative particle (*nañ*) does not indicate an object when preceded by a word such as "non-existent."
"Because of the application [of the same logic].
Or rather, the fault is equal; for how can there be a negation?
It should be explained that since the negation of that which does not exist is itself negated by you."
How is there a negation? He says: "asati" and so forth. Or, if this non-existent relation is negated, then like that [relation], the substratum (*dharmin*) which possesses the relation...

For when there is a statement of negation such as "there is no jar here in this place" or "it is not now the time," the cognition arises that there is no connection of the jar with this place or this time.
Likewise, when it is said, "the jar does not exist in this way," the cognition arises that the jar does not possess this attribute (*dharma*). This being so, when such a cognition exists...

Regarding the passage beginning with "tathāpi" and so forth, the opponent asks: even by means of the passage beginning with "nedānīm" and so forth, how is the relation negated, given that for this person neither the relation nor its property exists?
5 /// ... the notion that "there is no property" is in fact a negation of the relation itself, because it is the relation between the property and the substratum that is being negated.

Although the relation is spoken of as distinct—due to the difference characterized by conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*)—it is either the relation or the property [that is negated]. Furthermore, for this notion that "there is no relation," there is no possibility whatsoever of its existence (*sattā*) in a positive sense.
Why? [It is said:

"In the case of non-existences," and so forth. The word "tathā" (thus) implies the sense of "yathā" (as), because of the constant connection between the relative pronouns *yat* and *tat*. Just as when places and so forth exist, there is the non-existence of the cognition that "[it] does not exist."
Because it contradicts the cognition of an existent intrinsic nature (*satsvabhāva*).

The cognition that "this is not here" and so forth would not occur in the absence of those [objects], that is, in the absence of the cognition of their relation; or, if it were to occur, it would belong to that person who possesses such a cognition—just as there is a cognition of the absence of relation corresponding to the cognition of the absence of those objects. Thus, for one who possesses the cognition, it exists in accordance with that cognition.
By what can those relations— which have the absence of relation as their nature and have the absence of relation as their object— be prevented from being the very objects of conceptual construction?
They are indeed the objects of conceptual construction.
There is no relation [of denotation] for words...
7 /// It is not the object of sounds; however, the meaning is that a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) whose object is incomplete is necessarily an object of sound.
If those [conceptual constructions] have arisen, they are *vitarkas*.
But is there not a conceptual construction such as "this is blue" with respect to blue and so forth situated directly in front?
Since the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not the object of verbal expression, he says "for not," and so forth.
The "ineffable object" refers to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); since the context concerns discursive thought (*vitarka*), conceptual cognitions (*vikalpabuddhi*) are understood [here].
They "strive toward" means they take it as their objective support (*ālambante*).
[This pertains to] the general form (*sāmānyākāra*).

However, this conceit of those of dull intellect— that there is a simultaneous occurrence of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the mental aspect (*ākāra*)— is a mere conceptual construction.
This has already been examined by the author of the treatise in the *Pramāṇaviniścaya*, and thus it is not elaborated upon here.

The objection should be stated as follows: "How then is its inexpressibility [as a relation] asserted by the teacher Dignāga? To this he replies with the words beginning "of the relation" (*saṃbandhasya*).
"In its own form" means "in the form of a relation"; for a relation (*saṃbandha*) is that which relates (*saṃbandhana*).
The characteristic is mutual dependence.
Mere existence (*bhāvamātra*) is devoid of substantial reality (*asatvabhūta*),
and there is no word that denotes it by means of such a form.
A word denoting a relation must be accepted as expressive; and that [word] has been employed. [The question arises: "Of which two?"—thus there is an inquiry.
The relation is the cause for the cognition of the distinctness [of the relata]; at that time, it is perceived in the form of a related entity.
Thus he says: "In the expression [of the relation] as a related entity," and so forth.

When one says "the relation between the king and the man," the relation appears to the intellect as a related entity, as if its form were extracted from the king and the man, which are independent of each other.
Just as there is no cognition [of the relation] according to one's intention in the case of "the king’s man," so too the relation characterized by mutual dependence cannot be known...
3 /// ... [it is] only in the form of a relation according to the stated rule;
it is not denoted by its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*).
Therefore, there is no undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) regarding the relation even on account of non-existence (*abhāva*).

The meaning is as follows: while it must be stated that non-existence (*abhāva*) is made an object of cognition by the intellect, such expressibility (*vācyatva*) does not likewise apply to the relation. For non-existence is made an object of cognition by the intellect in its own form, and it is expressed by the word in exactly that same way.
The connection...
It is also stated [in the *Śābdikādhikaraṇa*]:
"Because that which has assumed the form of a related entity (*saṃbandhin*) alone is made the object [of cognition], and because it is non-different [from it];
thus it is said: 'The relation, being of a non-substantial nature (*asattvabhūta*), its form is not perceived; nor is there any denotation of the relation in its own form.'"
Therefore, it is established that the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) must necessarily be expressible.
Consequently, if there is the notion that no [real] connection exists, then the word arising from that [notion] nevertheless proceeds; and thus, it has non-existence as its object.
If the making [of something] non-existent is not accepted, then in the case of "there is no jar here," what is being negated? It cannot be the location and so forth, because that exists;
nor can it be the relation, because its absence is not perceived. Thus, this argument is trivial.

Furthermore, to one who asserts that non-existence is the denotable object, this proponent of the non-denotability of non-existence replies: "Non-existence is not expressible. How could one who does not speak [of it] provide such a rebuttal?
For indeed, by one who does not utter the word "non-existence," its [the object's] inexpressibility...
... [it] would be stated by that very word "non-existence" (*abhāva*).
How could it be so? Because non-existence itself is not admitted.
If it is argued: "Non-existence does not exist at all; therefore, because of its non-existence, there is no mention of non-existence," he says:
Now, regarding the passage beginning with "athābhāvam eva" (or "then [it would be] non-existence itself"): "by that" means by the non-connection of non-existence;
"now" means when non-existence is non-existent.
If that very thing is non-existence, how could there not be the use of the word "non-existence" in the statement "non-existence does not exist"?
It would somehow have to be so; otherwise, how...?
If it is argued that [the word] is merely a negation of an absence imagined by others, then at least the word must be admitted to have absence as its object.
Therefore, for one who in some way initiates the conventional usage of absence, it is necessary to admit that cognition and words necessarily have absence as their object.
As for what was further stated regarding the negation of an object:
Because one does not employ words that are devoid of meaning, for this reason, a negation (*nañ*) that lacks an object is not employed; the answer to this will be stated hereafter:
"That which arises from conceptual constructions produced by beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*)."

P Pramāṇavārttikaṭīkā r1 /// [This is] because, since non-existence lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), words that express the form of non-existence are not even to be suspected of expressing an intrinsic nature; for those words, having non-existence as their object, are established as denoting exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) or the "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*).

Regarding those words whose function or operation consists in referring to a real entity (*vastu*), what is their denotable form? Is the entity denoted in a positive form (*vidhirūpeṇa*), or rather... [the text is incomplete]

...because it is impossible for that [exclusion] to exist in the absence of the existence (*sattā*) of that form—the form which is to be apprehended, to be made an object, and which constitutes the intrinsic nature (*vastu-svabhāva*) of the entity.
"The existence of that form" is *tadbhāva*;

an entity whose characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is precisely that is described as such. This very thing is the primary exclusion (*viveka*), the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), which is the absence of all entities.
Of that discernment (*viveka*), which makes known its state as it truly is, [the phrase] "having the nature of discernment" ...

...the connection. Those words and conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) have as their basis a single entity that serves as the locus of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*); those words and conceptual constructions for which such is the case are described in that way.

For indeed, by means of the exclusion of the "unproduced," whatever entity is the locus of the word "produced" or its conceptual construction, that very same [entity] is the locus of the words and conceptual constructions such as "impermanent" and "selfless."
The connection is that even though they have become such [as described], their objects are indeed distinct.
Why? "According to each" and so forth.
That exclusion which [arises] from... [the rest of the sentence follows].
...of the exclusion characterized by non-eternality, such as "eternal" and so forth.

By those various divisions according to their respective limits, the distinctions among the exclusions of non-eternality and so on are conceptualized and accumulated. Through those distinctions, [these exclusions] appear in the conceptualizing cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) as if they were distinct entities within the various exclusions.
Because those words and conceptual constructions, while appearing [to consciousness], are perceived;
that is, because they are respectively conjoined as the signifier (*vācaka*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*).

5 /// Even though there exists the relationship of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) between these two, there is no conjunction (*saṃsarga*) or identity (*ekatva*) between the probandum and the probans; therefore, the fault previously stated—that if the essential nature (*svabhāva*) were the probandum, the reason (*hetu*) would be a part of the meaning of the thesis (*pratijñārthaikadeśa*)—does not apply. Thus he says:
"That is not so," and so forth.
The word "tad" means "therefore.
The connection is that "this very intrinsic nature" [is what is meant].

When it is pointed out as a reason—that is, when it is being stated—it is said to be dependent on a distinction of conditions (upādhi), which is to say, dependent on a distinction of qualifiers (viśeṣaṇa).
Or [it is] merely [known] through dependence on a qualification...

When impermanence is to be proven, "being produced" (kṛtakatva) depends on a distinction of conditions, whereas "existence" (sattva) does not. By the words "depending [on conditions]" and so forth, he states that being produced depends on a distinction of conditions. Since a real entity is unestablished for the opponent, the very capacity to produce it is what constitutes the operation of another.

And dependence (*apekṣā*) is precisely the conformity to positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). When its own nature is being produced, it depends upon the operation of another as the cause for the production of that nature, by which [nature] exists...
Even though [the word "produced"] expresses its own nature (*svabhāva*), because it is conditioned by something else (*paropādhi*), it implies this nature as a qualification of another.

By the phrase "by this"—that is, by the demonstration that being produced depends upon a distinction in conditions—the term refers to that which has the property of being differentiated by the distinction of conditions (*pratyaya*), namely the causes (*kāraṇa*). Thus it is "of such a nature."
The state of being that is "differentiation by the difference of conditions" (*pratyayabhedabheditva*);
for sound is differentiated by the difference in causes such as place and effort.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [qualities] such as being the immediate consequence of effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) are explained.
These also are the causes...
8 /// Thus,
the conclusion is made with the words "in this way" and so forth.
"In some cases" refers to the application [of the term].
[The term] "dependent on the distinction of limiting conditions" [is used].
For this very reason, the two words [denoting] the causal relationship in general are [stated] when the probandum is precisely "impermanence," just as existence [is stated].
And the analysis of the compound is: "this is both an intrinsic nature and a specific property."
By including that [intrinsic nature], it is stated in the present context that intrinsic nature is sometimes called a "reason" (*hetu*).
As in that very same case, when impermanence is to be proven,
even though it is the intrinsic nature itself, it is perceived as a specific property (*dharmaviśeṣa*).
Because manifestation is perceived as a specific property (*dharmaviśeṣa*) [of the entity],

there is no perception of mere intrinsic nature (*svabhāvamātra*) in its purity, as there is in the case of existence (*sattā*). Even when it has become an entity, it is perceived as a specific property.
Because manifestation is perceived as a specific property (*dharma-viśeṣa*) [of the entity],

there is no perception of mere intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-mātra*) in its purity, as there is in the case of existence (*sattā*). This intrinsic nature, too, should be understood as being dependent upon limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

In cases such as "being produced," the qualifying condition (*upādhi*) is something distinct [from the subject], whereas here the specific property (*dharmaviśeṣa*) is indeed identical with the [subject] itself; this is the only difference.
"By this direction" means by the direction of the classification of reasons that depend upon qualifying conditions.

The subject (*dharmī*) is established in its general form, while [its existence] in a specific form is what is to be proven (*sādhya*); this is the logical principle (*nyāya*). In that context, if "existence" refers to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) called "being," then even an intrinsic nature such as "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth would be included; therefore, [the qualification] is for the purpose of excluding those.
The mention of "existence" (sattā) is for the purpose of including its own-nature (svabhāva), since some maintain that existence is distinct [from the thing itself].
The meaning is that existence is the very self-nature [of the thing].
If the reason (hetu) is the nature of existence, then existence itself is not being proven [as something separate].
How could it be something to be proven?

Now, if it is thought that if existence-in-general (*sattāsāmānya*) were the object of proof, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established; therefore, a specific instance of existence (*sattāviśeṣa*) is the object of proof, and when that is being proven...
...the example [would be flawed]. Consequently, existence would not be proven.

In that case, even if the reason (*hetu*) exists, because the specific property (*viśeṣa*) does not follow [in the example], the example would be devoid of the means of proof (*sādhana*). Therefore, he says: "For there is no following," and so forth.
The deviation of the specific properties (*bhedānām viśeṣāṇām*) is contradicted; it is defective.
"Hetu-sādhayoḥ" is a locative dual;
the meaning is "in the reason and in the probandum," and "elsewhere" refers to [attributes] such as non-self (anātman) and so forth.
"Tad" refers to "being" (sattva).

The word "kila" indicates that this is not accepted [by the author]. "Being thus established" means [established] by such arguments as "the Pradhāna exists," and so forth, regarding the Pradhāna and other [principles].
It cannot be established.
Why? Because that specific quality lacks positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
As the teacher Diṅnāga said: "As it has been stated..."

Regarding what the Sāṃkhya has stated—that by the words "there exists the *pradhāna*," the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the *pradhāna* itself is established—that is contradicted and rendered faulty because of an ignorance regarding the object of inference as a means of valid cognition;
for inference has a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, and does not have a specific characteristic as its object. What, then, is contradicted? It is the [proponent's] reason (*hetu*) as well.
Because the fault is equal [in both cases], he says that very thing: "It is not a reason," and so forth.
...so he said; "therefore," and so forth.

"Therefrom" means from the uncommon reason (*asādhāraṇahetu*). "Existence" (*bhāva*) is being (*sattā*); that which has this as its substrate (*upādāna*)—that is, its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*)—is the subject (*dharmin*), and thus [the compound] is explained.

The word *mātra* is used for the sake of restriction; thus, [the subject] is merely qualified by existence (*sattā*). If the probandum were such a general property (*sāmānyadharmin*), nothing at all would be established for the Sāṃkhya.
Since the definition characterized by the three *guṇas* and so forth is unestablished, it has thus been stated that the proof is futile due to the unestablished nature of its own locus;
this applies to the opponent as well.
"... refers merely to a generality;
by this, it is stated that what is already established is being sought to be proven.
Alternatively, not a single object would be established.

And such [a thing] is unrefuted; for the word "and" (ca) has the sense of "because," meaning that since such a thing is unrefuted, no object is established due to the fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). He explains this with the words "it might be" (*syāt*) and so forth, beginning with "not in every way" (*na sarvathā*).

"In the proof of existence" (*sattāsādhane*) means in the establishment of existence (*sattāsiddhau*). "Having existence alone as its qualifier" (*bhāvamātraviśeṣaṇa*) means having mere existence as its qualifier (*sattāmātraviśeṣaṇaḥ*),
that whose specific qualification is not specified.

7 /// ... However, that proponent [asserts] that, in such a general way, nothing exists at all; thus, without touching upon—that is, without taking into account—any particular distinction (*bheda*) or specific property (*viśeṣa*) of this subject (*dharmin*), by that proponent, in this case where a distinction has been accepted, there is a subject whose specific property has not been accepted. In this subject, such as *pradhāna* and so forth, which is to be proven as having its distinction accepted through such [attributes] as "consisting of the three qualities" (*triguṇātmaka*) and "eternal" (*nitya*).
It would be a reason lacking positive concomitance (*ananvaya*).
It is "lacking positive concomitance" because there is no observed concomitance of this [reason] with the specific property to be proven (*sādhyaviśeṣa*) in the example;
that is, the example is devoid of the property to be proven.
8 /// ... [it is called] *ka* because it consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion (*sukha-duḥkha-moha*).

Even though it is such, it is held by others to be either one and partless, or something else endowed with agency and so forth; "in whatever way" means characterized by the aforementioned properties, whether collectively or individually; "of that nature" means a nature distinguished by the aforementioned qualifications.
And that subject (*dharmin*) is likewise [established], because there is no dispute regarding mere existence (*sattvamātra*). — *Pramāṇavārttikaṭīkā* 9 /// .. .. ti.
It has been stated [by us] that [the probandum] exists through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
For instance, the mere existence of fire and so forth—either unqualified by any particular substratum or qualified by a specific substratum—is what is to be proven (*sādhya*).
In the first case, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
Regarding what was said, beginning with "tatrāpi" and so forth:
"yatrāpi" refers to when fire and so on are the probandum (*sādhya*). In the second alternative, the example would be devoid of the probandum; thus he says "viśiṣṭa" and so forth.
A distinguished receptacle wherein fire and so forth [are placed]...

[The opponent argues: "There is non-establishment [of the reason] because there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) of that which is intended [as the locus]. For fire, which is connected to one substratum (*ādhāra*), does not exist in another substratum. The Teacher replies: "No. That substratum, which is intended as the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), does not qualify that fire and so forth. Wherever there is smoke, there is the universal of fire (*agnisāmānya*); and here there is smoke; therefore, the universal of fire exists even here. Thus [he says].

If [the property] is not qualified by its locus because only the universal is perceived, then how can it be [designated] as "a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*)? Thus, [it must be] qualified...

... because of the qualification [of the property] by the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of that [other], it is "only a property of the subject" (*pakṣasya dharma eva*), but not "a property of the subject alone" (*pakṣasyaiva dharma*). This was stated previously, and it will also be explained in the commentary on this verse—"the property of the subject is pervaded by its part"—in the fourth chapter.
"Therefore" is the conclusion.
"Therein" refers to the location and so forth.

"By the exclusion of non-connection with that" means by the exclusion of the non-connection of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) with that locus (*dharmin*), such as the location and so forth.
And therefore, because the universal is being proven, [it is not...]

If it is argued that even in a subject (*dharmin*) such as *pradhāna*, what is to be proven (*sādhya*) is mere existence (*sattāmātra*) by means of the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), he replies: "It is not so here either.
Why? Because in certain cases—namely, in subjects such as *pradhāna*—the very object denoted by words like *pradhāna* is absent, being characterized by the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) and so forth;
thus, that existence would be entirely without qualification.
"Because of the absence of a substratum that serves as a qualifier.
[The opponent asks: "How so? and so forth.
"[There are] many properties such as existence (*sattva*), knowability (*jñeyatva*), and so on..."

Since those [qualities] such as being knowable are accepted as having the nature of reality (*dharmatva*), that [subject], such as *pradhāna*, is already established; it is only in respect to that [established subject] that "existence-in-general" (*sattāsāmānya*) is being proved.

Here too, when the subject is conceived in the form of being knowable and so forth, it cannot be conceived as a single entity consisting of pleasure and so on, characterized by specific attributes such as permanence;
for it is precisely such a specific attribute that is the object of proof.
Therefore, it must be established by this [argument] that there exists something knowable...

Even though the point that "it exists" without qualification is established, [the opponent might argue] that the existence of *pradhāna* and so forth may still not be established. For there is no dispute regarding the mere existence of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*). To this he says, "Nevertheless," meaning that what is intended is certainly not established. The sense is that something specific would have to be established.
"In another case" refers to such applications as "there is fire here because of smoke," and so forth.
"Devoid of that" means a lack of connection with that particular location; the meaning is that there is a lack of connection with that specific place.
That universal which possesses this [quality] is described as such; that is to say, it is connected with a specific location.
Thus, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of that which is connected with a specific location is simply not established.
He refutes [the objection] with the words "no," etc., because a universal does not subsist elsewhere.
Indeed, no one...
... [it is] necessary to show that [the presence of fire] is inseparable from smoke, like fire which is never found without smoke. By what kind of statement should this be shown?
He says: "Wherever there is smoke, there is fire," etc. This means that the smoke is "thus" (tathā) by way of demonstrating a pervasion (*vyāpti*) that encompasses all cases.
Pervaded by fire alone, the established [subject] is seen right where it exists within its locus (dharmin) in its own form as smoke, with the causes of error having been dispelled; therein indeed...

3 /// ... when [the reason] is understood through inference, there is no purpose whatsoever in stating the probandum (*sādhya*), because the probandum is established even without it. He says that very thing with the words "In that case" (*tatra*) and so forth. In that case, regarding the general subject (*sāmānyadharmī*), there is the perception of the mark (*liṅga*); and from the mere statement of its connection with the subject of the probandum (*sādhyadharmin*)—that is, the connection characterized by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—[the probandum is established].

Since the desired probandum is established, and since there is no mention of the subject (*sādhyadharmin*) at that time, then in the absence of such a mention, how could there be [an inference] characterized by it?

Since this smoke has been established as being inseparably connected (*avinābhāvī*) with the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), namely fire, wherever it is perceived in a particular location, it—by the very nature of things (*arthāt*)—excludes the non-connection of that location with fire;
that is to say, it establishes that the location possesses fire.
For this reason, that location is said to be "thus" (*tathā*), meaning it is the locus of the probandum (*sādhya*) by virtue of possessing fire.
This is because it arises subsequent to the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
it is not, however, preceded by such a formal presentation [of the reason], as in the case of fire connected to a specific location.

5 /// ... [it is] so. Furthermore, since the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) must necessarily be preceded either by the presentation of the thesis (*pakṣa*) or, if it is to be preceded by that, by the presentation of the thesis—given that this is established by logic—who could possibly set aside the thesis from the proof? For at that time, the statement of the thesis itself also functions as a constituent of the proof.
And since it is not so, therefore this is established:
the pervasion of the logical mark (liṅga) by means of the generality of the property to be proven is to be stated even without explicitly showing the subject (pakṣa).
This is the teaching of the venerable Ācārya Dignāga.
Thus he says: "And likewise," and so forth.
The non-deviation of the mark (liṅga), such as smoke and the like, however, is with respect to the property to be proven (sādhyadharma).

"Elsewhere" means in another [locus] that excludes the connection with a specific subject (viśiṣṭadharmin), that is, in a mere subject (dharmimātra) whose particular substratum has not been apprehended.
Others, however, explain that [the property] is seen elsewhere than in the subject of the thesis, namely in the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*). They...
R Pramāṇavārttikaṭīkā r1: ...the logical mark (liṅga) has not been shown there in the subject (dharmin) which is the locus of dispute;

[it must be] established, that is, ascertained, and endowed with that pervading property (vyāpaka-dharma), for being so endowed, it will cause one to understand the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin).
The conclusion is provided by the words "Therefore" and so forth.

As for what was stated— that just as there is the fault of lack of positive concomitance (*ananvaya*) when existence (*sattā*) is the probandum, so too is there such a fault regarding the reason— the response to that is given by the words "unconsidered" (*aparāmṛṣṭa*) and so forth.
... not grasping at anything else...
The positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the reason, which is "mere existence," is not obstructed in its occurrence within the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*).

To the question, "Of what kind of probandum (*sādhya*) when proving 'mere entity' (*vastumātra*)?", he says: "of that which pervades only that," meaning "of that which pervades mere existence. He explains this with the words "by means of the proof" and so forth.

When the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) pervades only the entity and no specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*) is grasped, and the proof is again applied as "existence," there is no violation of the positive concomitance; nor is there an example devoid of the proof.

The meaning is: even when relying on existence-in-general (*sattvamātra*) as the reason; it does not mean, however, that there is no reliance on the specific [form] of existence when it is the probandum (*sādhya*). Why? Because if mere existence were the probandum, the proof (*sādhana*) would be futile.
Having stated the fault regarding existence from the perspective of the probandum, he states it from the perspective of the proof:
Furthermore, and so forth:

when existence (*sattā*) is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), would a reason (*hetu*) be adduced as a property of an existent (*bhāvadharma*), or as a property of both an existent and a non-existent (*bhāvābhāvadharma*), or exclusively as a property [of one]? In that regard, if it were unestablished (*asiddha*) in the primary [subject]...
4 /// ... that [reason] is deviant (*vyabhicārin*) and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) when existence (*sattva*) is the property to be proven (*sādhya*).
Furthermore, whatever is a property of non-existence (*abhāva*), that is contradictory (*viruddha*) when existence is the property to be proven, because it proves the very opposite of existence.
And how can that existence be proven, for which—as existence is the property to be proven—there is no reason at all due to faults such as being unestablished (*asiddha*)?
"Having that as its cause" means having a reason that establishes existence; "that which has three members" refers to that class of faults, that nature of defects, which consists of three parts;
[the author] does not [fall into] it as far as possible.
5 /// ... [The author] analyzes this very point:

For a property of an entity (*bhāvadharma*) being taken as a reason (*hetu*) must either consist of its effect (*tatkāryātmaka*) or be its own-nature (*tatsvabhāvabhūta*). First of all, the first position is not tenable, because the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) itself is unestablished. Indeed, the relation of cause and effect is established by means of perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*) through a specific cause; and that [specific cause] does not exist in the case of the Primal Matter (*pradhāna*). Furthermore, even the relation of cause and effect characterized by the absence of the effect when the cause is absent is not a cause. ///
6 /// ... because it possesses the nature of being an entity, a property of an entity (*bhāvadharma*) is called a reason (*hetu*).
How could that [reason] exist in respect to *pradhāna* and so forth, whose existence is unestablished?
For how could a proponent who desires a property of an entity as the reason in respect to that *pradhāna* and so forth not also accept *pradhāna* and so forth as an entity?

Because that very nature of an entity (bhāvasvabhāva) is its property (dharma). If it is asked, "How then is this expressed as 'this is the property of the intrinsic nature' using a term of distinction (vyatireka)? he replies:
"For the intrinsic nature itself," and so forth.
By what?

Having established the subject (*dharmin*) by means of the exclusion of other distinctions, and having again established that very same [subject] as a property (*dharma*) through the exclusion of other distinctions, it is indicated— by means of a word for which such a convention has been made— as if it were distinct, as if it had a different form from the subject,
in accordance with the desire of the knower.
And this has already been determined previously;
thus he says, "For not," and so forth.
This has been stated [in the passage] beginning with, "The exclusion and non-exclusion of other differences by those two," and so on.

[The opponent] says: "Even if it were a phenomenon of non-existence, it would still be a cause characterized by fear. To this, [the author] replies with the words beginning "anāśrita" (unreliant), etc.
This is what he means:
If it were argued that [the absence] is stated by accepting a positive phenomenon (*dharma*) according to the rule,
or by the negation of one [thing], [it would refer to] the nature of the portion of a real entity (*vastu*) which is the opposite of that;
yet there is no contradiction in this, because even in the case of the absence of that which is imagined as a phenomenon consisting merely of the negation of another object, there is no opposition.

In this context, by the mention of "exclusion" (vyatireka), one sets aside the property (dharma) presented through the mode of affirmation; by the mention of "mere" (mātra), one sets aside that which consists of the objective aspect (vastubhāga) obtainable through negation as a means. Why does it become "mere exclusion" alone? He says:
"by non-exclusion" (aparyudāsena); for affirmation has negation as its subordinate element, whereas exclusion (paryudāsa) [is the opposite].

Regarding the phrase "not based on a real entity" (*anāśritavastu*): where something is resorted to by way of excluding other things, that is the domain of *paryudāsa* (prescriptive negation). However, in this case, no real entity whatsoever is resorted to; rather, he says "no" and so forth to indicate mere exclusion.

That is to say, "it is not material"—thus, immateriality (*amūrtatva*), which is characterized by the negation of materiality, would apply even to a non-entity (*abhāva*) that lacks any designation (*nirupākhya*), and so on.
The point is this: negation is indeed cessation. And that [cessation] is an action; furthermore, an action is not possible without a substratum for the action.
Therefore, non-existence is not a negation.

This is the intended meaning. [Objection: But have not words been shown to apply even to non-existence (*abhāva*) in the intervening discussion? [Response: True, it has indeed been established that even that which lacks any designation (*nirupākhya*) can be the object of negation; however, this was stated from the perspective of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) on the grounds that a negative particle (*nañ*) cannot be employed without an object. This present point, by contrast, is distinguished by its approach through the relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākārakasambandha*).
If that which is indefinable (nirupākhya) cannot be the object of a negation, then why should it not now be the object of an affirmation? ... [ta]t... // 127 //
The objects [of negation] are precisely the objects of negation.
Why? Because of the statement "of affirmation," and so forth.

That which is the cessation of affirmation is itself negation, because there exists nothing other than affirmation and negation. Furthermore, there is no such thing as a cessation that is a real entity (vastubhūta) or an action, by virtue of which [negation] would not apply to non-existents.

How could this aforementioned mere exclusion (*vyavacchedamātra*), which is possible in both the case of existence and non-existence, appropriate to itself the status of being a prover when existence is the probandum? For... [the text is incomplete].

In that case, there is doubt; by the exclusion of that [doubt], when "existence" (sattva) is the probandum, non-existence (asattva) is the counter-example (vipakṣa). And for a reason (hetu) that possesses both properties, there is no exclusion from the non-existent counter-example. Furthermore, that proponent, by his own speech—that is, by his own statement—is asserting that the reason which establishes existence possesses both properties.
He states that the reason (hetu), which possesses both properties, functions even elsewhere, whether [the property] exists or does not exist;
for it would possess both properties only if it were to function both when [the property] exists and when it does not exist. [Regarding] existence...

If this proponent were to speak of existence (*sattva*) [as a property] of that which is non-existent (*asat*), his reason (*hetu*) would be contradictory (*viruddha*), because he would be establishing non-existence, which is the opposite of existence. To the question, "What, then, is a property of non-existence itself?
he says: "In mere existence," and so forth.
For that object which pervades mere entities— characterized by such features as causal efficacy (*arthakriyākāritva*), being produced (*kṛtakatva*), and so forth—
its exclusion is necessarily a property of non-existence alone;
for the negation of all existing things is itself nothing but non-existence.
"...only non-existence," and so forth, [indicates] that existence resides only in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).

"That" means for that reason; this threefold cause, as it has been divided, has no other course for establishing existence—that is, for proving existence—than these three types of causes as they have been divided.
"In the state of a proof" (*sādhanatve*) means in the state of being a logical mark (*liṅgatve*).

Because this existence, by virtue of not having its specific qualities grasped in a general sense, [resides] in a subject (dharmin) whose existence is already established as the locus of the thesis...
S: By this, the fault of being unestablished (*asiddhatā*) has been avoided. Avoiding both contradiction (*viruddhatva*) and inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*), he says:
"And by that," and so forth.
By that property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the logical mark (*liṅga*).

If this is ascertained "in some way"—either by way of positive concomitance (*anvayamukha*) or by way of negative concomitance (*vyatirekamukha*)—then there are no contradictions or deviations (*vyabhicāra*).
There is neither contradiction nor inconclusiveness; this undesirable consequence does not apply to existence.

When the locus (*pakṣadharman*) or the basis of the reason is not ascertained, or when the pervasion (*vyāpti*)— which must be ascertained by virtue of being of that same nature— is not ascertained regarding the nature of the subject (*dharmin*) that serves as its basis, then whatever is intended to be a prover (*gamaka*) is not a prover at all; for this very reason, such a cause [of proof] is invalid.
The reason (*hetu*) must be stated as being pervaded by its own property (*svadharma*), namely the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*),
and as having an established nature within the subject (*pakṣadharmī*).
The meaning is that it must be stated with its three characteristics (*trairūpya*) ascertained.

... [the lamp] being perceived, such a lamp—when existing inside the interior of a jar or the like—is sometimes incapable of cognizing that [jar's] form; thus, it does not perform its own functional activity (arthakriyā), which consists in the illumination of pillars and so forth. If such is the nature of the indicator (gamaka) as described, then what is the nature of the indicated (gamya)?
To this he says: "It is the pervader of that," and so forth.
That which is the pervaded nature, the indicator, has its pervader ascertained.
The dharma is that which is to be understood.
Of what nature is that [reason] which is intended as the means of understanding, being certain by virtue of its pervasion? Furthermore, how does it become certain by virtue of its pervasion?
He says: "Precisely from the ascertainment of that property."
The ascertainment of that property [as the probandum] occurs through its nature as a property that makes [the probandum] known;
the meaning is that the ascertainment of that property arises precisely from the ascertainment of the probans as having the nature of a means of proof (*sādhana*).
By this much, the relationship between the follower and the follower-of has been stated.
Having gazed...
5 /// [When] its own cessation occurs, it is the negator of that pervaded; he explains this with the words "of that" and so forth.
The connection is as follows: this pervading property (*vyāpaka-dharma*), while ceasing of its own accord, is the negator of that pervaded (*vyāpya*).
What is the reason? Because in this way, this pervading property of his is established as the probandum (*sādhya*).
"If, in the absence of this pervader (*vyāpaka*), the pervaded (*vyāpya*) were not to exist"—
the word "that" (*tad*) is used here for the purpose of introducing the statement.
"By this" (*anena*) refers to what was just mentioned, [namely] the subject (*anuvartya*) and the correlate (*anuva...*).

It should be understood that the definition of the means of proof (*sādhana*)— which consists of the application of a syllogism possessing either similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*)— has been stated as the characteristic of being a prover (*sādhaka*) of the probandum (*sādhya*), according to their respective order.
He states that very twofold nature of the syllogistic application in the passage beginning with "For it is twofold," and so forth.

As the Naiyāyikas say: "There is only one [type of] syllogism; for that which possesses positive concomitance (*sādharmya*) is the *anvayin*, and that which possesses negative concomitance (*vaidharmya*) is the *vyatirekin*. But is it not the case that the distinction between the *anvayavyatirekin* (the mixed) has been established otherwise? That whose absence from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) does not exist, and which exists only in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), is the *anvayin*; whereas that which is strictly excluded from the dissimilar instances due to the absence of similar instances is the other [the *kevalavyatirekin*].
Because positive concomitance (anvaya) is impossible; for without positive concomitance, there can be no negative concomitance (vyatireka).
"Because it follows from the exclusion of others, it is called both positive (anvayin) and negative (vyatirekin).
This must also be accepted by them on the basis of the nature of things (vastubala).
Establishing this very point, he says "of these two," and so forth.

"Of these two"—that is, of the reasons characterized by positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—there is in reality, in terms of their essential nature, no difference whatsoever, because both possess positive and negative concomitance; the only difference lies in the distinction of their formal application (*prayoga*).
Those same positive and negative concomitants are at times demonstrated by a formulation possessing positive concomitance...

If it is argued that in a formulation based on similarity (*sādharmya*) only similarity is understood, and in one based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) only dissimilarity, and therefore [the other] must also exist [there], that is not so; because even in a formulation by way of similarity, the exclusion of the reason from the counter-example of the probandum (*sādhyavipakṣa*)—which is dissimilarity—is understood through the force of the meaning (*arthāt*), that is its capacity (*sāmarthya*). It is this very capacity that [the verse] expresses with the words "it does not exist," and so forth.

"In that" refers precisely to dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). For the reason would be pervaded by the probandum (*sādhya*) only if there were no connection with the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyavipakṣa*). Since the term "dissimilarity" expresses this [absence of connection], he asks: "How is there an understanding of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in that case? To this he replies with the words beginning "if not," etc.
[If] the reason were pervaded in such a way, it would indeed be excluded by the exclusion of that [probandum].
And this we shall explain in detail in the investigation of the negative reason (*vyatireki-hetu*).

Regarding the phrase "just as the effect [is] with respect to impermanence," the meaning is that "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) exists only where there is impermanence. And this is an example of the positive concomitant (*anvayin*).
"Non-produced" means "destructible.

Since there is an absence of being produced (*kṛtakatvābhāva*) and an absence of destruction (*vināśyabhāva*), it is indestructible; therefore, this is the meaning: when there is an absence of destruction—that is, when it is indestructible—it is non-produced, [and thus] uncreated...
"...and so forth. 'Of these two' refers to the positive and negative [reasons].

'Whatever it may be' is a statement of universal pervasion (*vyāpti*); from that, by implication, follows the exclusion of permanence from what is produced, which constitutes the understanding of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
For in this way, everything produced would be impermanent if there were nothing permanent whatsoever for which [permanence] is indeed eternal."

If it is argued that since that [property] does not exist, how could there be exclusion from it? In that case, there is no doubt at all, because in the absence of that [property], [the reason] does not occur therein.
...anticipating this doubt, he says "of the state of being produced," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "when the state of being produced is stated [in respect] to sound": when the state of being produced—which is pervaded by impermanence—is stated in respect to sound, it necessarily brings its own pervader (impermanence) into proximity; thus, by the very force of the implication, it follows that "sound is impermanent."
"Therefore, not necessarily," and so forth; the connection is "there is no necessary specification.
"Here" refers to the application of the method of agreement (*sādharmya-prayoga*).
He states a formal argument (prayoga) that possesses the property of non-identity;
it is also a negative inference (vyatirekin).
The phrase "sound is produced" (*kṛtakaś ca śabdaḥ*) is the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*);
here too, there is no statement of a proposition (*pratijñā*).
Because, since its non-existence is established by way of its being established as having that nature— namely, the nature of impermanence acting as the instrument—

when there is an absence of impermanence, neither [the reason nor the subject] exists; and when the existence of "being produced" in sound is proclaimed— that is, when its presence is made manifest by stating "sound is produced"— then, for that which exists with such a nature...
"...because it is established that 'sound is impermanent' through the application of similarity (*sādharmya-prayoga*) as previously stated.

[Objection: But in the formulation 'the state of being produced does not exist in the absence of impermanence,' only the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) has been stated, and the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) has not been stated. To this he replies with the words 'But the positive concomitance... and so forth. The impossibility of dissimilarity without positive concomitance is *arthāpatti* (presumption); he expresses that very point with the words 'For not... and so forth."
"Of that which is not restricted to having that as its nature" means [of that which does not have] impermanent intrinsic nature.

... [it is] precisely that which is necessarily restricted; upon the cessation of that [cause], there is the cessation of that [effect]. Since this is so, therefore, having established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) characterized by identity (*tādātmya*), one must state the cessation of the reason (*hetu*) through the cessation of the probandum (*sādhya*).

Now, is it not said that the exclusion [of the probans] follows from the exclusion of the probandum for the very purpose of establishing the rule? If the rule has already been established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), what is the use of this fruitless statement regarding exclusion?
7 /// ... having established [the positive concomitance], the exclusion [of the reason from the dissimilar instances] is subsequently stated.

Regarding this, as for what one says—that the statement of exclusion is for the purpose of demonstrating the restriction—that is not so; because the statement of exclusion is for the purpose of removing the suspicion of the reason's occurrence in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), but by it the relation [of pervasion] is not expressed.
Because the absence of the reason is understood from the word [of the treatise] when there is an absence of the probandum;
identity (*tādātmya*) is one thing, while non-existence in the counter-example (*vipakṣāsattva*) is another—there is someone who does not understand this.

... [it] is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, [the word] "it ceases through its cessation" refers to the restriction (*niyama*) that "if this [word] is established," [then the object must cease]. The commentary [explains] "occurring at a later time" as the meaning of "the state of being restricted to that very nature" (*tadātmaniyama*).
T Pramāṇavārttikaṭīkā r1: Others explain it differently: "The restriction (*niyama*) is that the means of proof (*sādhana*) exists only when the probandum (*sādhya*) exists.

And the word "having established" (*prasādhya*) is, by implication, a statement of an entailment (*ākṣepavacana*); therefore, the meaning is: "Having established that restriction, [the means of proof exists]."

Having implied the restriction (niyama) through the force of the sense, the exclusion (nivṛtti) must be stated; thus, by such a statement, that exclusion which implies the restriction through its own capacity must be expressed—precisely for this reason he says: "And that... [sā ce... etc.

By that statement, the restriction to its own nature (tadātmaniyama)—that is, the restriction to the nature of the probandum—is implied by the force of the expression (uktisāmarthyāt) through the sense [of the argument]. For this reason, the positive concomitance (anvaya) is established.
How so? And so forth.

For the opponent indeed accepts that what is produced is necessarily subject to destruction; however, he maintains that it persists for some duration of time. Therefore, the meaning of this question is as follows:
"Since what is produced is necessarily impermanent due to its destruction immediately after arising, how is it to be understood that it [persists] for another period of time?"

... [it] is said to be produced and to perish immediately after arising. Let it be granted that impermanence follows from being produced; however, momentariness is not established. To this he replies with the words "because," and so forth.

"From its own nature" (*svabhāvāt*) means from the very existence—that is, the arising—of its own produced form; the meaning is that the nature of impermanence is established precisely at the time the nature of being produced is accomplished.
"Its existence" (*tadbhāva*) refers to the existence of impermanence...

...of things that are perishable and have impermanence as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), [perishability] follows from their very nature; this is the explanation of the phrase "because it is connected to its nature," starting with "since it is thus" (*yata evam tasmāt*). "By its very nature" (*prakṛtyaiva*) means by its very essence (*svabhāvenaiva*). If, however, destruction were caused by something else, then it would not necessarily occur. Showing this very point, he says: "of those things that are dependent," and so forth. Therefore, an entity is independent regarding its destruction; the word "ca" (and) serves to emphasize this restriction.
"...would be the cause of their destruction. If it is argued that because the causes of destruction are numerous, there is no place where they are not present, he says 'by which,' etc.
'By which' means for what reason. 'From that cause' means from the cause of destruction."
The connection is that even for those causes of destruction, there is not necessarily a presence [of them].
Why? Because their presence is dependent upon their own conditions (*svapratyaya*), since they depend on the presence of their own causes; and it is not the case that [destruction occurs] without...
6 /// ... because of the non-presence of the cause of destruction, nothing at all would be destroyed.

However, since destruction is certain through the presence of that [specific] cause—given that causes do not necessarily possess their effects, nor necessarily possess the effect called "destruction"—why [is this so]?
Because of the deficiency [of conditions], etc.; that is, due to the deficiency in the presence of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*).
Obstruction is the occurrence of something contrary.
By this [it is shown that] for that which is dependent, there is no necessary occurrence.
(Margin, line 8)
Regarding those [logicians] who maintain that the causes of destruction serve as the inferential marks (*liṅga*) for destruction:
why [is this not so]? Because the effect is not established; that is, because there is no rule that the cause of destruction necessarily produces an effect whose nature is destruction.
To whom, then, does this undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) apply? He says: "those who hold [destruction] to be produced," and so forth.
"Having a cause" (hetumantam) ... [7] ... / The conclusion is by means of the words "that" (tat) and so forth.
"That" (tat) means "therefore" (tasmāt).
Furthermore, this is the meaning:
that which is produced is independent with respect to its own existence—
that is, with respect to the state of destruction.
[The state] is determined by the nature of non-destruction;
by this, the fruit of the proof [is established].
As for the impossibility... that [is] so stated because of the final totality of conditions (*sāmagrī*).

What, then, is the obstruction to its arising? He says: "complete. The meaning is that it is fulfilled by means of auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*) and the transformation of the continuum (*saṃtāna-pariṇāma*).
By this, the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) has been stated.
The formal argument (*prayoga*), however, is as follows:

those things which are independent with respect to a certain state are necessarily restricted to that state, provided there is no possible cause for an obstruction; for example, [as in the case of] a seed that is unimpeded by obstacles.
"… [the reason] ‘destruction is [inherent] in them’ is a *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason).
With the words “But surely,” etc., he raises the objection of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*).

The meaning is that even for certain causes that are independent with respect to some effect, the existence of that effect is not necessarily certain; thus, where there is independence, there is no rule regarding the necessity of that effect’s existence.
To the question "Where, then, is this [stated]? he says "the stages," and so forth.
For that [causal capacity], when it exists in such a state, is independent in producing its effect; yet, even while it exists, the sprout is sometimes not produced at the time of obstruction.
And this [is explained in the section on] the continuum...

3 /// ... [there is] no certainty [in that]. Because the transformation of the continuum (*santānapariṇāma*) in the aforementioned totality (*sāmagrī*) depends [on other factors] for the production of the effect, the reason—that [the continuum] is independent [of such factors]—does not apply there. [The opponent might argue: "Even for a produced thing (*kṛtaka*), there is a waiting for another time (*kālāntara*) with respect to its destruction; therefore, the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*. To this he replies: "It is not so," and so forth. For a produced entity (*bhāva*), there is no dependence whatsoever on another time for its destruction.
For if it were so, then because intrinsic nature is without distinction, it would not exist later either, just as it was before.
"Because [the causes] depend on other factors, the reason is indeed inconclusive. To this he says, "In that case as well," and so forth.

The earth, seed, and so on do not possess a single intrinsic nature (ekasvabhāva), for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the effect would be produced even before, just as it is afterwards. Rather, they are distinct through successive transformations (pariṇāma). "In that" refers to that causal complex (sāmagrī) which is differentiated by the transformation of the continuum (santāna-pariṇāma).
The final factors are those that arise last; they constitute the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) which is capable of producing the effect in the very next moment.

5 /// ... Among the transformations (*pariṇāma*) mentioned immediately above, [one might ask: "What is the purpose of the first transformation, or how is it said to be the cause? To this he says, "But another," and so forth. He states that there is yet another, distinct from that final transformation which is considered the producer; that is to say, there is something else beyond it.
"Prior" means "for that purpose," which signifies the moment of capacity;
and thus, because it is the cause of the cause, it is designated as a "cause" by way of metaphorical usage.
Regarding the example, he says "and not," and so forth.
"That" refers to the final causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

"Therein" means when the effect is to be produced; [the phrase] "existence in one place" refers either to the arising of a transformation within the final moment that constitutes the cause, or else—because that final moment would lose its unity due to the departure of the preceding [moment] known as the transformation.
And because a second [moment] arises, it would therefore not be the final one. Now, if [you argue that] this fault must not occur...

7 /// ... [of that which is] comprised within the moment [and] not performing a deficiency regarding the production of the effect—that is, the production of the effect—U *Pramāṇavārttikaṭīkā* r1 /// ... in the case of the effect, namely, when a rice-sprout is to be produced.
Why is that? Because even in the case of barley seeds and the like, the conditions for their production—such as soil, water, and so forth—are sometimes present there;
yet, even when those conditions are present, they do not produce a rice sprout.
Therefore, the state of affairs remains inconclusive.
"How so? asks the proponent of the established tenet (siddhāntavādī).
The meaning is that these [entities] are indeed dependent.
...the connection [is as follows]:
"dependence on that intrinsic nature" means dependence on the intrinsic nature of producing a rice sprout.
And since the cause does not operate therein [in the case of the non-rice seed], there is no inconclusiveness (anaikāntika).
"In that case, then," says the opponent.
With reference to both types of causes—the dependent and the independent—he says, "of certain produced things" or "of certain existing things"; here too, the word "certain" is connected [to both].
That very nature which is perishable does not exist.
moment by moment...
"Because they depend on their own perishable nature, they are not perishable.
By this, he states that the reason "because of independence" is unestablished (*asiddha*).

He refutes this with the words "the rice seed," etc.; by the word "etc.," [he includes] barley seeds and so forth. That is their nature: the nature of producing or not producing an effect that is either desired or otherwise.

On the grounds that it arises from its own cause: whatever is a barley seed and so forth, if it is not the cause of that [rice], it is not the cause of that for which it is not the cause—namely, the rice seed.

Regarding one who thinks that there is no differentiation of causes at all because [the effect] is not distinct from its nature, he says in response: "And it possesses a determinate capacity," and so forth.
That which has a determinate (*niyata*)—that is, a differentiated (*pravibhakta*)—capacity characterized by a specific excellence of its own nature is "possessing a determinate capacity.
Such a thing is a cause, such as the seeds of rice or barley which produce their respective effects.

For "the state of being derived from the primary elements" (bhūtabhautikatva) is not accepted as a single, unitary form; moreover, the distinction between causes is perceived through direct observation. Thus he says: ... [etc. ...

"...by this [it is] established," he says, beginning with "nor... and so forth. The "determination of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things" (arthānām padārthānām) means that they possess distinct intrinsic natures.
Why is it not logical for [this determination] to be "accidental" (*ākasmika*), i.e., causeless? He says: "of that which is independent," and so forth.

For that which is independent of causes, [the production] occurs only in a certain place and not everywhere, at a certain time and not always, and in a certain substance such as barley seed and the like, and not in all substances.
This is the one who...
6 /// ... from [this] place and so forth, it is understood that existence possesses a cause; for the conventional usage of "possessing a cause" is based solely on this much. This is a *svabhāvahetu*.

Just as there is a restriction of nature (*svabhāvaniyama*) in the case of rice seeds and the like due to a difference in causes, so too here, in the case of things that are produced (*kṛtaka*) or existent (*sat*), a restricting cause must be stated—by which restricting cause these things are [determined to be] produced and existent.
Or some are born with perishable natures, while others are not.
7 /// ... those [things] which are all produced from causes alone; the meaning is that their destruction is established by way of a specific distinction.
And this should be understood as having been stated with reference to destruction at a later time, which is indeed acknowledged by the opponent himself.
