But this is not for the purpose of establishing its destruction at every moment, since that is what was under discussion; rather, once destruction is established even after an interval of time, its perishable nature is proven, otherwise it would remain as it was before even afterwards.

8 /// Because [the cause] does not exist [as a permanent entity], one who desires that a non-perishing self (*anaśvarātman*) produces a cause must admit that it produces something that persists for all time.

And such a produced thing does not exist; for everything, after some interval of time, v1 /// ... as [the case with] cognitions, sense organs, and bodies, which are perceived as having their continuity severed... trees and so forth, as well as mountains and so forth, also perish precisely due to the destruction of the trees and other things supported by them; otherwise, there would be no destruction of that which is supported.
Because they belong to that same class, it is established that even other things—including diamond and the like—undergo destruction, since at times even the effect of consciousness does not arise;
thus, the distinction between perishable and imperishable is not determined by their causes.

2 /// ... its nature is birth; that very [nature] does not exist [in another], thus it is perishable. This is what is meant: for some, birth itself is of such a kind that one thing becomes perishable while another does not. Indeed, birth is not the cause of a perishable nature. For there is no such thing as "birth" existing separately by which it could make something have a perishable nature. For the birth of entities is their very nature; it is precisely that [nature] whose differentiation by causes is being examined.

...the accomplishment of [one's] hopes; nor is birth the cause of that which has destruction as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, among produced things (*kṛtaka*) or existent things (*sat*), there is no differentiation of intrinsic nature based on whether a cause produces something perishable or imperishable. Because that [differentiation] is absent, there is an absence of differentiation among causes; and consequently, for an effect—whether it be produced or existent—there is no differentiation by way of being perishable or imperishable. Thus, it is not the same as the case of barley seeds and the like.
...due to dependence on being produced...
... because that [existence] has been accepted [as a property]. This is not so, because existence is incompatible with that which is unproduced (*akṛtaka*).

For all existence is restricted by place, time, and substance; if there were no cause, such restriction would be impossible. Since atoms (*paramāṇu*) and the mind (*manas*) possess form (*mūrtimat*), their restriction to a specific location is accepted by the opponent. In the absence of any assistance provided by that [cause], how could an atom exist in this particular place?
Not in another [way]... thus...

5 /// ... [He] summarizes the meaning of the formal argument beginning with "therefore" and so forth—namely, that those things which are independent with respect to a certain state—by means of the phrase "this independence of destruction," etc.
What does this independence of destruction do? It acts as an opponent to the existence of destruction at any place or at any time.
Some establish the non-existence of that—namely, the non-existence of its state of destruction—by means of its own nature, that is, by its existence.
6 /// ... [at] that time or in that substance, it would depend upon that time and that substance; thus, it would not be independent at all. This was stated previously.
"Then that [is the case]," says the opponent.
"No," says the Master.
Because it arises in that very way—from the fact that existence itself serves as the cause—there arises a perishable nature.
Clarifying this very point, he says: "For of that which exists," and so forth.
If it is argued that an entity arises from some cause, this is the intended meaning: not every existent thing is dependent upon a cause.

For some existents, such as space, time, and atoms, are indeed eternally immutable (*kūṭastha-nitya*). Consequently, the reason "because of existence" (*sattvāt*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to those very things.
[The term] *ākasmikī* means being without a cause (*ahetuka*).

V. *Pramāṇavārttikaṭīkā* r1 /// ... Why? Because the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is determination; that is, because their fruit is ascertainment (*niścaya*). For even perception (*pratyakṣa*), though it is a means of valid cognition, even when grasping all aspects (*sarvākāra*), [is only a means of valid cognition] with respect to those aspects for which it produces ascertainment...
... [omitted] ... n. cey. ... [omitted] ... ///

The analysis of the compound is: "that mind which has non-determination as its characteristic. The meaning is that when doubt exists, the mind does not form the certain resolve, "one must certainly not act.

[Objection: Since even from doubt people such as farmers sometimes do engage in action, how then can this [non-perception] be said to have non-engagement as its result, and thus be authoritative? To this, he says:
If that were the case, then that... [would follow].
3 /// ... this non-apprehension of an invisible object is said to have non-occurrence as its result.

Regarding the phrase "arising from a preponderance of the mark" (*liṅgātiśayabhāvinī*): the "mark" (*liṅga*) is non-apprehension; its "preponderance" (*atiśaya*) is a specific distinction (*viśeṣa*), namely that [the object] has reached the conditions for apprehensibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*).
Its "existence" (*bhāva*) is its being present (*sattva*).
That [locus] in which this exists is described as such;
the meaning is "possessing a specific characteristic" (*liṅgaviśeṣaṇavatī*),
up to and including "having the conditions for perception" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*).
[The term] "of one who has attained" arises from this qualification.
[The author] explains it with the words "here," and so forth.
"Here" refers to the conventional usage of the non-existent (*asadvyavahāra*).

"As previously illustrated" refers to [the passage] beginning with "certain [non-apprehension] has the non-existent as its cognitive result, depending on a distinction of reasons," and so forth. Furthermore,
as for what was stated [earlier], that "non-apprehension is not a means of valid cognition":
It should not be understood without distinction; rather, it is [the nature] beginning with "svabhāva" and so forth.
The state of being remote in terms of place and so on is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for those two.

The meaning of the whole passage is as follows: "There is no means of valid cognition regarding the probandum" constitutes the absence of perception, which is the non-cognition of the essential nature (*svabhāva*);
the absence of inference is the non-cognition of the indicator (*jñāpaka*).
This principle has been illustrated in reference to the cessation of both perception and inference when the object is imperceptible.
He explains by means of the passage beginning with "yasya" (of which):

the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of any object whatsoever that is remote—due to the cause of remoteness in terms of place and so forth—is not perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). That intrinsic nature... [thereafter].

6 /// ... [it is] not non-existent merely by the cessation of perception, as was stated previously; nor is there, in the case of remote objects, the capacity to produce cognition through the appropriation of its own causal efficiency, and so forth. Having thus explained the "non-cognition of the intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvājñāna*), he says "even that which...
and so on, desiring to explain the "non-cognition of the indicator" (*jñāpakājñāna*).
The phrase "of the indicator" (*jñāpakasya*) is an elaboration of "of the mark" (*liṅgasya*).
An object that is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*) is rejected;
for instance, that there is no one who is entirely dispassionate (*virakta*).
7 /// ... or is it rejected?
Here, a specific qualification is rejected, not the mere existence of the subject (*dharmisattāmātra*), as in [the statement] "there is no giving" and so forth.
Furthermore, "giving and abstention from violence" is a *dvandva* compound.

The volitions having those [actions] as their objects are likewise so described; that is to say, the volitions of giving, and the volitions of abstaining from harming. "Being the cause of prosperity" means being the cause of distinguished future fruits.
In this context, it is not the intrinsic nature of the volitions themselves that is being rejected... [text fragment].
8 /// ... because [the nature of] volitions is perceptible, they are the cause of spiritual progress (*abhyudaya*).
Since that [nature] is their very essence, it is indeed perceptible; so from where does this delusion arise?
To this he says: "Even with respect to an object that is perceptible," and so forth.
The connection is with the phrase "even regarding an object that is directly perceived, one is mistaken.
He says "he might even deny" (*apavadet*), meaning he might even reject;
[this refers to] "that fruit," and so forth.
Those specific volitions which have no such fruit— that is, those which do not result in higher rebirth (*abhyudaya*)—
are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
If it is asked how there is similarity by virtue of similarity with them, he says:

Because there is no immediate succession of the fruit: those volitions which have other fruits and those which have that [specific] fruit—in both cases, the immediate succession of that fruit is not observed;
therefore, it is not so because of the lack of immediate succession of the fruit.
...because effects that are separated [from their causes] by an interval of time are observed through a process of successive transformation of states; "mūṣikā ca ālarkaś ca" is a *dvandva* compound;
"ālarka" refers to a mad dog;

from the poison produced by the bite of a mouse (*mūṣika*) or a mad dog (*ālarka*), even though no change was previously seen, after an interval of time, [the effect] characterized by fainting and so forth [is observed].
Because a transformation is observed—in the case of rat poison and the like, since a transformation is subsequently observed—it is logical to infer the capacity for that result.
He says that it is precisely the existence of a sentient being (*sattva*) that is logical,
beginning with the words "That," and so forth.

In this regard, because there is no contradiction regarding the existence of a fruit in the future arising from volitions such as giving, and because there is an absence of any subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), [it is established].

If mere non-perception is not a valid means of knowledge when the probandum is the absence of the capacity to produce an effect, and if there is no subverting proof [to the contrary], then there is no denial of its existence; what proof is there for its being? There is indeed no proof. Therefore, it is true that even the ascertainment of its existence is not tenable; for this very reason, [there is] the subverting [proof].
... thus, there would be no rejection [of the claim] that there might be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the omniscience of one whose mind is dispassionate.
And that possible means of valid cognition will be explained in the second chapter.

This might be the case: if the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) characterized as the cause of prosperity belongs to the volitions (*cetanā*) of abstaining from harming, then when those [volitions] are apprehended, that [nature] too would be apprehended; yet it is not apprehended.
And when one thing is being apprehended, that which is not apprehended cannot be its intrinsic nature (svabhāva).

[Objection: "Since [an object] is not seen, it follows that it does not exist because it does not perform a causal function (*arthakriyā*); this will therefore constitute a sublation (*bādhaka*). [Response: To this he says, "In this regard," and so forth.
The word "that" (*tat*) is used to introduce the statement.

The word "here" (*atra*) is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), meaning: "among these aforementioned remote objects, of certain objects or of certain intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*)," and so on.
Nevertheless...
Because of its non-existence, there is an absence of the capacity to produce a determination of the nature of an object exactly as it was perceived;

thus, for certain objects that are remote in terms of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth, the effect would fail to serve as a signifier, and due to that absence, the signifier would be unestablished.
To the question, "Why is the effect itself absent? he says:
"Of causes," and so forth.
For indeed, [a cause] does not [arise] from itself... [etc.]
Because [the object] has not become an object of perception for those with limited vision (*arvāgdarśana*),
it is "not to be inferred" merely by the absence of the aforementioned means of cognition.

Regarding the phrase "its non-existence," this refers to the non-existence of specific intrinsic natures (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*) of supersensuous entities (*atīndriya*), such as particular deities and so forth.
... [based on] direct perception and inference ...
8 /// ... in some cases, because of the dullness of vision, the nature that has been seen is not determined. ///

Just as substances such as poison [are transformed] through practice, so too, for yogins in whom the light [of wisdom] has manifested, the manifestation of volitions such as generosity is possible; and regarding the attainment of the yogins,
we shall state the proof that is possible.

Likewise, it is observed that for certain seeds and other things whose effects have not yet begun, the production of their effects occurs after a lapse of time; let this possibility be conceived even in the case of supersensible entities. For instance, [it is seen that] piśācas and the like [act] upon certain...
[The opponent argues: "Neither is there a proof of non-existence through the non-perception of the effect, nor is there a non-perception of the cause;
for even in that case, it is the non-perception of the cause that proves non-existence. To this, [the author] replies with the words "But regarding the effect," and so forth.

However, regarding an effect that is remote from its own nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth, the non-cognition of the causal agent—namely, the non-perception of the cause—is indeed the means of proving non-existence; this he explains by the words "own nature" (*svabhāva*) and so on.
When the non-existence of a remote object's own nature is to be proven, the non-apprehension of its own nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*) alone is the [valid] means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

...the perception [of the effect] itself cannot be ascertained; for those things that are remote by nature and so forth, it is impossible to ascertain with anything at all a relationship of cause and effect. This is true; however, regarding the apprehension of a mere absence of the object specified, one can say this much:
without a cause, an effect—though remote by nature and so forth—necessarily does not exist.
The presentation of this has been made by way of such a brief summary;
for that very reason, it is...

4 /// ... even that which has an unindicated object can be established. [Objection: "Is this not so? and so forth—the opponent argues. Because smoke is seen in a dwelling house and the like even when fire has perished, there is thus a deviation (*vyabhicāra*), since an effect is observed even in the absence of its cause.
By the statement "In the absence of a cause, the effect would not exist," the meaning is that the effect exists at the time the cause exists;
that is, as long as the cause has existence, so long does the effect have existence. We do not say this in such a way that... [text truncated]
There would be the consequence [of the effect persisting] because an effect that has arisen once remains for a further period of time even after the destruction of its cause.
To the question, "What then is expressed by this statement? he says: "Devoid of a cause," and so forth.
Although this [point] is separated by the text beginning with "tathā" and so forth, nevertheless, the meaning...
When the cause has perished, there is no longer even a possibility for the effect to exist; so how can there be any suspicion of deviation?
For instance, that momentary instance of smoke which is produced by fire cannot persist once the fire has perished.

This is because in the very second moment in which the smoke-moment produced by the fire exists, the fire-moment that serves as its cause has already perished, and immediately thereafter, in the third moment, the smoke-moment [ceases].
"...is also destroyed," thus [he said]. / ku... /

Showing that [the smoke] has fire as its cause, he says: "And not in that way," and so forth. "Abiding in that manner" means that even when the initial cause has perished, that which endures for a period of time and takes that [fire] as its material cause—that is, taking as its material cause a previously ceased cause—how then is it that smoke is later said to have fire as its cause?
To this he says: [the following].
"Successively," and so forth.
First, fire alone produces the initial moment of smoke; that moment of smoke [produces] another, and that too [produces] another...
3 /// ... because it gives rise to what is considered [the effect]. It is designated as its effect;
that is, even though it is posterior, it is designated as the effect of that first cause.

If the non-existence of this reason were somehow established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then its effect—the effect of that very reason being negated—would be determined to be non-existent;
thus, its absence would be cognized by some [means of] reason, as will be stated in the following passage.
4 /// ... However, in the case of an unindicated object, it is not considered in this way;

for [the opponent] merely intends to establish that "if the cause were not present, the effect would necessarily not exist, because the arising of an entity devoid of a cause is impossible," and this has already been stated immediately prior in the passage beginning with "svabhāva" (intrinsic nature).

Regarding the phrase "of the object": when the non-existence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) within the nature of the sign-bearer (*liṅgin*), which is the probandum (*sādhya*), is to be established, there is both the non-perception of the nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*) and the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*).
He explains [the passage] beginning with "its very nature" (*svabhāva eva*).
"Something" (*kiñcit*) refers to the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*).

If the pervading nature of this intended object of negation, which is the pervaded (*vyāpya*), were established as being unperceived, then it would be a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), just as, for example, when the pervader "treeness" (*vṛkṣatva*) is established...

[Pramāṇavārttikaṭīkā r1] ... [the object] would be cognized by some reason called the non-perception of its own nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*). By the words "if," etc., he states the meaning: the connection is that "if the absence of this causal factor were established.

And the absence of the pervading nature (*vyāpaka-svabhāva*) is [established] from some indicative reason (*gamaka-hetu*), namely, from the non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta-anupalambhāt*). For that very [non-perception] is the means for negation... [text fragment].
... because the non-establishment of the absence of the cause and the pervader results in doubt regarding the effect to be negated and the pervaded as well.
This should be understood as applying to the proof of the absence of the object under discussion, as previously stated.

If it is argued that when the absence of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is to be proven, only its non-perception (*anupalambha*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), then how, in that case, is the absence of an entity such as a jar established through its own non-perception?
He states the answer: "Of the visible..."
In the margin (line 7):
He does not say that there is no remoteness from intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
For such a thing, which exists as unperceived, its "existence" (*bhāva*)—that is, the absence of existence (*sattā*)—is cognized.

"When there is no possibility of a cause for the non-perception [of an object], what could be the cause of that non-perception?"—this refers to the absence of other causes; when such [other causes] are impossible, it means "when all other conditions for perception are present.
He explains this with the words beginning "For existence... and so forth.
It is called a *bhāva* because it brings itself into being and makes itself manifest.
It is a specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*) that is not remote from its own inherent nature.

If such a thing were to exist, it would necessarily be perceived by its respective perceiving cause—that is, by whichever sense faculty is the perceiver of that object. By this, the phrase "of the visible" (*dṛśyasya*) as previously stated is explained.

In the presence of conditions for perception—such as the absence of obstructions and so forth (the word "and so forth" including deficiencies, hindrances, and the like)—it is indeed perceived, and not otherwise.
Thus, that which is of such a nature yet unperceived is determined to be non-existent. Why? Because such a thing, being existent, has met the criteria for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*).

Because perception is non-deviant, this very reason—which was stated as "the determination of the absence of the nature of that which is perceptible through its being seen," and so forth—is indeed [the proof]. // [End of verse] //

"...and of that which is contradictory," and so forth; here the word "ca" (and) is displaced in its order and should be understood as applying to "and upon the perception of that which is contradictory to it.

That is to say, when there is the perception of something contradictory to that by whose absence the probandum is established—namely, when there is the perception of that which is contradictory to it—there would be the ascertainment of non-existence, i.e., the absence of the object to be negated. For what reason? Because [the object to be negated] exists where there is the existence of the contradictory thing.
Because its existence is sublated;
that is to say, because the existence of that which is intended to be negated is sublated, due to the non-coexistence of two substances.
This is what is expressed by the passage beginning with "yo hi" and so forth.
He explains:
for whatever entity [exists] by means of which...

... [he] says: "Of those two substrata," and so forth. Of those two opposites, that which is their substratum (*upādāna*), there is a mutual [relationship]; by virtue of being the basis for that, the substratum of cold is the basis for the deficiency of the substratum of heat, and the other is the basis for the other—this is the meaning.
For that reason, because there is a contradiction in the simultaneous commencement of the effects of the opposites, cold and heat, in a single location.
Of those two, in the manner just described...
In the classification of [non-perception], [it is said]:
"There is no sensation of cold here because of fire," and so forth.

Although there is no explicit mention of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) here, nevertheless, this logical mark (*liṅga*) called "contradiction of essential nature" (*svabhāvaviruddha*) is not stated as something separate from non-perception.

What is the reason? Because contradiction is understood precisely from that non-perception, and because non-existence is established through contradiction. For how could a contradictory [thing] be ascertained if, upon the perception of that [subject], there were no non-perception of its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*)?

The meaning is that because the non-existence [of the object] is not established due to the non-apprehension [of it], non-apprehension itself is employed as a contradictory indicator (*viruddhavyabhicārin*). Let it be granted that the cognition of non-existence arises from such a non-apprehension whose object is perceptible, and therefore this is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); however, the point is: how is this inference (*anumāna*), or rather, is it indeed a distinct means of valid cognition? This is the intended sense.
"How could it not be so? asks the Teacher.
"Because it does not depend upon an example," says the opponent.
For inference depends upon an example, [involving] positive and negative concomitance...
[The author] states "not so" (*na hi*) and so forth, showing that [the argument] does not depend on an example.

Regarding the word "in this" (*asyām*), meaning in non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), the Master asks: "Why is it not 'unnameable' (*nirupākhya*)? and so forth; the meaning is that [this] is indeed an example.
"That is non-existent" (*tad asat*) and so forth is the opponent's [objection].
How and by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is it to be understood that such things as a sky-flower are non-existent, such that this would be the case?
The meaning is that there would be an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) when non-existence is to be proven by the mark (*liṅga*) of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*).
[It is] from the mark of non-perception alone that [the non-existence of] a sky-flower...

The analysis [of the compound] is: "Is there an example for that proof of non-existence? Now, if another example were required here for that proof of the non-existence of a sky-flower and the like, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), because for that [second example] another would be required, and for that yet another, and so on.
And thus, since an infinite regress would ensue, there would be no comprehension even of a single thing;
therefore, in all cases, for the sake of avoiding the fault of infinite regress, [the cause] must be something indefinable (*nirupākhyam*).

"Even in such formulations as 'because there is no perception of that which has reached the characteristic of being perceived,' non-perception is not an inference because it does not depend on an example," says the Teacher [Dharmakīrti]. "Even though he hears it"— that is,

even though he hears what was stated once, namely, that in the case of the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), it is not non-existence (*abhāva*) that is proven, but rather the conventional usage of non-existence (*abhāvavyavahāra*).
The fool has three names: Deva, Divya, and Prajāyati; therefore, he is dear to the gods and to fools.
6 /// ... demonstrating that the thesis to be proven is precisely the conventional expression of non-existence, he says:
"For the sign," and so forth.
The non-perception of the perceptible is the non-perception of that which is capable of being perceived.

That non-apprehension is the sign and the cause of the conventional designations of existence; by its own presence—that is, by its own proximity—it [produces] its own signs, which are of the nature of that non-apprehension.
